parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> *IKEA *is a well-known home furniture retailer with stores throughout the world. It was started in 1943 by Ingvar Kamprad when he was given some money by his father for doing well at school. He wanted to produce furniture at a price that people could afford to buy.
> 
> He realised that transporting furniture to customers was difficult as goods were often damaged. He developed flat packs to avoid damage. A flat pack contained all the materials needed to self-assemble a table, a chair or a bed.
> 
> All *IKEA *stores are run as franchises.

A Canadian supplier of timber charges *IKEA *\$19.75 Canadian Dollars (CAD) per load.

The exchange rate is \$1 CAD = 6.58 Swedish Krona (SEK).

Which **one **of the following would be the cost to IKEA for 1,000 loads in Swedish Krona?

Select **one **answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**The correct answer is D — 129 955.00 SEK**

The cost in CAD for 1,000 loads is:

$19 . 75 \times 1  000 = 19  750  \text{CAD}$

Converting to SEK:

$19  750 \times 6 . 58 = 129  955 . 00  \text{SEK}$

**A** is incorrect as it divides only the number of loads by the exchange rate: $1  000 \div 6 . 58 = 151 . 98  \text{SEK}$

**B** is incorrect as it divides by the exchange rate instead of multiplying: $19 . 75 \times 1  000 \div 6 . 58 = 3  001 . 52  \text{SEK}$

**C** is incorrect as it calculates the total cost in CAD but does not convert to SEK: $19 . 75 \times 1  000 = 19  750 . 00  \text{SEK}$

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> *The Better Toy Store (TBTS)* is a children’s toy shop. *TBTS *has three shops in Singapore. Two of the shops are located in busy shopping malls and the third is located at the Jewel Changi Airport. *TBTS *has a website for customers looking to buy toys online.
> 
> *TBTS *selects toys to sell that are excellent for play, value, design and quality. All *TBTS *toys are environmentally friendly.

*TBTS *sells balloons in packs of four at a price of 67.60 SGD. 
The exchange rate is 1 SGD = 3.05 Malaysian Ringgit (MYR).

Which **one **of the following would a customer in Malaysia pay in MYR for 4 balloon packs?

Select **one **answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**The correct answer is D – 206.18 MYR**

The cost of 4 balloon packs in SGD:

$4 \times 67 . 60 = 67 . 60  \text{SGD}$

Converting to MYR:

$67 . 60 \times 3 . 05 = 206 . 18  \text{MYR}$

**A** is incorrect as it is the price of one balloon pack divided by 4, i.e. $67 . 60 \div 4 = 16 . 90$

**B** is incorrect as it is the price of four balloon packs in Singapore Dollars divided by 3.05, i.e. $67 . 60 \div 3 . 05 = 22 . 16$

**C** is incorrect as it is simply the price of one pack of four balloons in SGD, not converted to MYR

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> *NEXT *is a well-known clothing retailer that operates in 70 countries and employs over 43,000 employees. Since *NEXT *commenced trading it has introduced many other products to its range such as home interiors, flowers and a wedding list service.
> 
> In 1999 *NEXT* launched its own online shopping platform, enabling customers to purchase its products where ever they live. It continues to improve its customer service by introducing new initiatives such as next day delivery.
> 
> *NEXT* mainly uses its own factories for production. However, it does purchase some clothes such as ladies dresses from Turkish factories.

*NEXT *purchased 5,000 dresses from a Turkish manufacturer at 101.10 New Turkish Lira (TRY) per dress.

The exchange rate is £1.00 (GBP) = 6.74 (TRY)

Which **one **of the following would *NEXT *pay in £ (GBP) to the Turkish manufacturer for the 5,000 dresses?

Select **one **answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**The correct answer is D**

The total cost in TRY is:

$5 , 000 \times 101 . 10 = 505 , 500  \text{TRY}$

Converting to GBP:

$505 , 500 \div 6 . 74 = 75 , 000  \text{GBP}$

**A** is incorrect as 5,101 is calculated by adding 5,000 + 101.10

**B** is incorrect as 5,674 is calculated by adding 5,000 + (100 × 6.74)

**C** is incorrect as 33,700 is calculated by multiplying 5,000 × 6.74

> **[case-study]**
> *Artify Studio* was set up in 2015 by Tay Hui Jae in the busy Kampong Glam area of Singapore.* Artify Studio*’s aim is to have ‘a communal art space where people can come together and paint, where people would be given as much creative freedom as they would have if they were in their own spaces.’

> *Artify Studio* provides many services including its popular Liberty Art Jam where customers can paint as well as listen to music. The studio offers a Corporate Art Jam and Regular Kids Classes. Customers can purchase art materials after attending the studio.

> *Artify Studio* is a profit-making organisation with a social element. It employs seven part-time people, all of whom are art enthusiasts.

*Artify Studio* imports sets of acrylic paint from Malaysia at a cost of 8.50 Malaysian Ringgit (MYR) per set.

The exchange rate is 1 MYR = 0.33 S\$ (SGD).

Which **one **of the following would *Artify Studio* pay in SGD if they imported 15 sets of paints?

Select **one **answer
parts.solutionMd:
**The correct answer is D**

The cost of 15 sets of paint in MYR:

$15 \times 8 . 50 = 127 . 50  \text{MYR}$

Converting to SGD:

\$\$127.50 \times 0.33 = 42.08\,\text{S\\$}\$\$

**A** is incorrect as this is the result of dividing the cost of one set (8.50 MYR) by the number of sets (15) and then multiplying by the exchange rate, or a similar miscalculation

**B** is incorrect as this only converts the cost of one set of paint into SGD without accounting for the 15 sets ($8 . 50 \times 0 . 33 = 2 . 81$), then possibly applying a further error

**C** is incorrect as this is simply the number of sets ordered, ignoring the cost and exchange rate calculation

> **[case-study]**
> *The Alternative Drum School (TADS) *was set up in the wealthy area of Cricklade, England in 2008 by Ollie Tanner who had a passion for and enjoyed drumming. Ollie invested all of his savings into the drumming school. He saw the potential of being located away from other drumming schools.
> 
> Ollie promotes his business by writing columns in local papers, performing at local music festivals and by word of mouth recommendations. He has invested heavily in computer technology to allow students to produce the music they enjoy playing.
> 
> Ollie finds it difficult to maintain a good work-life balance. Ollie currently works 60 hours a week in a business that does not have reliable profits.

*TADS *has developed contracts with drumming schools in other countries to teach online music lessons.

An Italian drumming school has agreed that *TADS* can teach five lessons per week. Each lesson costs £15 for half an hour. The exchange rate in January 2019 was £1 = €1.15.

What will the Italian drumming school pay in euros (€) for these five lessons?

Select **one** answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**The correct answer is D**

The total cost in GBP is:

$5 \times 15 = 75  \text{GBP}$

Converting to euros:

$75 \times 1 . 15 = 86 . 25  \text{EUR}$

The Italian drumming school will pay EUR86.25 for the five lessons.

**A** is incorrect as this is worked out by multiplying five lessons by the exchange rate of EUR1.15

**B** is incorrect as this is simply the cost of one lesson in GBP, not converted to euros

**C** is incorrect as this is worked out by multiplying the cost of each lesson at GBP15 by five lessons, without converting to euros

It designs and manufactures robots which are used in hospitals, hotels and restaurants. In hospitals its robots are used to move medical supplies between departments. (million) | > |---|---| > | Current assets | 12 | > | Inventory | 4 | > | Current liabilities | 7 | > > **Figure 3** Analyse the benefits for *Saha *of becoming a multinational business.

By manufacturing robots in all continents of the world, Saha would be able to sell its products to a much larger global market **[1 mark]**. Becoming a multinational would also allow Saha to manufacture robots closer to its customers in different countries **[1 mark]**. This would help the business to compete on price against rivals like NIO, Zoox and Vention **[1 mark]**, which is important as more businesses are entering the global robot market and competing for market share **[1 mark]**
> - Operating across multiple continents would allow Saha to spread its risk across different economies **[1 mark]**. > As We Grow (AWG) is a clothing business in Iceland. The social objective of the business is to use natural materials, such as wool, and produce environmentally friendly products. parts.solutionMd:

This will increase AWG's production costs for its jumpers, dresses, shirts and baby clothes **[1 mark]**, which could reduce profit margins unless AWG raises its prices, potentially putting off the families it aims to serve **[1 mark]**

However, a weaker ISK also means that AWG's clothing will become cheaper for international customers to buy **[1 mark]**. This could increase demand from overseas customers who purchase through AWG's website **[1 mark]**, helping to boost export sales and revenue, which is important for a business that only has one store in Iceland and relies on online sales to reach customers in other countries **[1 mark]**

> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for applying the impacts to AWG's context
> 
> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for explaining the impacts to the business
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Higher import costs may force AWG to look for cheaper alternative materials **[1 mark]**. However, AWG's social objective is to use natural materials like wool **[1 mark]**, so switching to cheaper alternatives could compromise its environmental values and damage the reputation that earned it the Icelandic Design Award **[1 mark]**
> - Increased export sales from the weaker ISK could give AWG the revenue needed to expand its product range further **[1 mark]**. With more income from international customers, AWG could invest in developing new products from leftover materials **[1 mark]**, supporting its aim of reducing waste while growing the business beyond its single store in Iceland **[1 mark]**
> 
> Answers that list six impacts on AWG of a depreciation of the ISK with no explanation will get a maximum of 1 mark

> **[case-study]**
> Vento is a bicycle manufacturer based in Milan, Italy. It employs 85 workers and exports 70% of its bicycles to countries outside the European Union (EU), including the USA, Japan and Australia. Vento imports lightweight aluminium from China to keep productin costs low. In the past year, the euro has appreciated significantly against the US dollar, Japanese yen and Australian dollar, but has depreciated against the Chinese yuan.
> 
> Vento's owner, Marco, is concerned about the impact of these exchange rate changes on the business. He is considering whether to start manufacturing in one of Vento's export markets to reduce the business's exposure to exchange rate fluctuations.

Evaluate the impact of the exchange rate changes on Vento. You should use the information provided as well as your own knowledge of business.
parts.solutionMd:
An exchange rate is the value of one currency expressed in terms of another currency. When a currency appreciates, it increases in value compared to other currencies **[K]**

The appreciation of the euro against the US dollar, Japanese yen and Australian dollar means that Vento's bicycles will become more expensive for customers in these countries to buy** [K]**. Since Vento exports 70% of its bicycles to the USA, Japan and Australia** [Ap]**, this could lead to a significant fall in demand as customers switch to cheaper competitors, reducing Vento's sales revenue at a time when these export markets make up the majority of its business **[An]**

However, the euro has depreciated against the Chinese yuan, which means that the aluminium Vento imports from China will become more expensive **[K]**.** **This will increase Vento's production costs for its lightweight bicycles **[Ap]**, squeezing profit margins from both sides as the business faces higher costs and potentially lower export revenue at the same time **[An]**

Overall, the exchange rate changes are likely to have a seriously negative impact on Vento **[E]**. The business is highly exposed because it relies on exports for 70% of its sales and imports its key raw material from China **[Ap]**. Marco's idea of manufacturing in an export market could help to reduce this exposure in the long term, as selling in local currency would remove the exchange rate risk on exports **[E]**. However, this would require significant investment that may be difficult to fund when profits are already being squeezed** [Ap]**. In the short term, Vento may need to absorb some of the cost increases and accept lower profit margins to keep its prices competitive and retain customers in the USA, Japan and Australia** [E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **12-mark 'evaluate' questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts linking points together to show clear cause and effect
>   - A clear, justified conclusion based on evaluation of the issues
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - The stronger euro could force Vento to lower its prices in export markets to remain competitive → this would reduce profit margins on 70% of its sales → potentially threatening the financial viability of the business
> - Vento could try to find alternative suppliers of aluminium in countries where the euro has not depreciated → this would help to control production costs → although the quality may not match the lightweight Chinese aluminium that Vento currently uses
> - The exchange rate changes may encourage Marco to focus more on selling within the EU where there is no currency risk → reducing Vento's dependence on exports to the USA, Japan and Australia → although this would mean entering new markets where the business may not have an established customer base
> - If the exchange rate changes are temporary, Vento may be better off absorbing the short-term impact rather than making costly long-term changes like relocating production → maintaining its current operations and customer relationships → until the euro returns to a more favourable level

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Solis is a solar panel manufacturer based in Porto, Portugal. It employs 120 workers and sells its products across Europe. Two years ago, Solis began exporting to countries in Africa, where demand for solar energy is growing rapidly. Solis currently manufactures all of its products in its single factory in Porto.
> 
> The African Union has recently formed a new trade bloc that removes tariffs on goods traded between its member countries. Solis is not based within this trade bloc. Several of Solis's competitors have already opened factories in Africa to take advantage of the trade bloc. Solis's owner, Carla, is considering whether to open a factory in a member country of the African trade bloc to remain competitive.

Evaluate whether Solis should open a factory within the African trade bloc. You should use the information provided as well as your own knowledge of business.
parts.solutionMd:
A trade bloc is a group of countries that agree to reduce or remove trade barriers, such as tariffs, between them **[K]**

Opening a factory within the African trade bloc would allow Solis to sell its solar panels to member countries without paying tariffs** [K]**. This is important because several competitors have already opened factories inside the bloc **[Ap]**, so if Solis continues to export from Porto it will face higher costs than its rivals, making its solar panels more expensive and less competitive in a market where demand is growing rapidly **[An]**

However, opening a factory in Africa would require significant investment in land, equipment and training new workers** [K]**. Solis currently manufactures all of its products in a single factory in Porto with 120 employees** [Ap]**, so Carla has no experience of managing operations across two continents, which could stretch the business's resources and lead to problems with quality control or production delays** [An]**

Overall, Solis should open a factory within the African trade bloc** [E]**. Demand for solar energy in Africa is growing rapidly, and competitors are already establishing themselves inside the bloc **[Ap]**. If Solis does not act, it risks being locked out of this growing market by tariffs that make its products too expensive compared to those manufactured within the bloc **[An]**. While the investment is significant, the cost of doing nothing could be greater, as Solis would watch competitors take market share that it may never be able to win back **[E]**. Carla could start with a small factory to limit the initial investment and scale up as the business establishes itself in the African market** [E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **12-mark 'evaluate' questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts linking points together to show clear cause and effect
>   - A clear, justified conclusion based on evaluation of the issues
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - A factory in Africa would bring Solis closer to its customers in the region → reducing transport costs for heavy solar panels that currently have to be shipped from Porto → helping to lower prices and increase competitiveness
> - Solis could benefit from lower labour costs in some African countries → reducing its overall production costs compared to manufacturing in Portugal → increasing profit margins or allowing it to offer more competitive pricing
> - Carla may struggle to find workers with the specialist skills needed to manufacture solar panels → training a new workforce takes time and money → and production quality may initially be lower than at the established Porto factory
> - Opening a second factory means Solis would be operating in a different legal and regulatory environment → Carla would need to understand local laws on employment, tax and manufacturing standards → which adds complexity and cost to running the business

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Wave is a surfboard manufacturer based in Peniche, Portugal. It was set up six years ago by Tomás and employs 20 workers. Wave sells its handcrafted surfboards to surf shops across Europe. The business has built a strong reputation for high-quality boards, and Tomás takes pride in personally overseeing every stage of production.
> 
> Tomás has noticed that demand for surfboards is growing rapidly in South America, particularly in Brazil. Brazil is a member of the Mercosur trade bloc, which removes tariffs on goods traded between its member countries. Wave currently pays a 15% tariff on all surfboards exported to Brazil.

Tomás is considering two options to grow sales in South America:

- Option 1: Continue exporting surfboards from Portugal to Brazil and absorb the 15% tariff.
- Option 2: Open a small factory in Brazil to manufacture surfboards within the Mercosur trade bloc.

Justify which one of these two options Wave should choose
parts.solutionMd:
A trade bloc is a group of countries that agree to reduce or remove trade barriers, such as tariffs, between them. A tariff is a tax placed on imported goods, which increases the price for the buyer** [K]**

Continuing to export from Portugal means Tomás can maintain full control over the quality of every surfboard **[K]**. He currently oversees every stage of production personally** [Ap]**, so staying in Peniche ensures the high-quality reputation that Wave has built over six years is protected, which is what attracts surf shops across Europe** [An]**

However, the 15% tariff makes Wave's surfboards more expensive for Brazilian customers** [K]**. As demand for surfboards is growing rapidly in Brazil **[Ap]**, Wave risks losing potential sales to competitors who can manufacture within Mercosur and sell without the tariff, making it difficult for Wave to compete on price in this growing market** [An]**

Opening a factory in Brazil would allow Wave to sell surfboards within Mercosur without paying the 15% tariff** [K]**. This would make Wave's prices more competitive in Brazil and across other Mercosur member countries **[Ap]**, helping the business to take advantage of the rapidly growing South American market and significantly increase its customer base beyond Europe **[An]**

The drawback is that opening a factory in Brazil requires significant investment, and Tomás would be managing production across two continents** [K]**. With only 20 employees currently in Peniche, the business may not have the resources or experience to set up operations in a new country **[Ap]**. Tomás would also be unable to personally oversee production in Brazil, which could lead to a drop in quality that damages Wave's reputation **[An]**

Wave should choose Option 1 **[E]**. The business's strongest asset is its reputation for high-quality handcrafted surfboards, built over six years under Tomás's personal oversight **[Ap]**. Opening a factory in Brazil risks compromising this quality and stretching a small business too thin. While the 15% tariff increases costs, Wave could pass some of this on to customers who are willing to pay a premium for a high-quality European-made board **[Ap]**, rather than risking the brand on a factory Tomás cannot directly control** [E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Exporting from Portugal means Wave does not need to invest large sums in a new factory → keeping costs low and the business financially secure → which is important for a small business with only 20 employees
> - The 15% tariff may become unsustainable if competitors within Mercosur offer similar quality surfboards at lower prices → Wave could gradually lose its share of the growing Brazilian market → missing the opportunity to establish itself before the market becomes saturated
> - A Brazilian factory would bring Wave closer to its South American customers → reducing shipping costs for bulky surfboards that currently travel from Portugal → and allowing faster delivery times which could improve customer satisfaction
> - Tomás may struggle to find skilled craftspeople in Brazil who can match the quality of his handcrafted boards → training new workers takes time and the results may be inconsistent → which could lead to customer complaints and damage the reputation Wave has built across Europe

parts.problemMd:

It aims to design clothes that will last a long time, to encourage families to buy fewer clothes and reduce waste in society.
> 
> AWG’s increasing product range now includes jumpers, dresses, shirts and baby clothes. These are produced in small workshops that employ family and friends. Waste is kept to a minimum and any leftover material is used to make scarves and hats. The business has one store in Iceland. It uses its website to advertise and sell its clothing online to customers in other countries. The business has received the Icelandic Design Award for its contribution to the environment.

Evaluate the impact on *AWG* of having these social objectives when planning to grow the business. You should use the information provided as well as your own knowledge of business.
parts.solutionMd:
A social objective is a goal set by a business that aims to benefit society or the environment rather than focusing solely on profit **[K]**

Having social objectives can help AWG to grow by strengthening its brand image and reputation **[K]**. By using natural materials like wool and reducing waste, AWG has already won the Icelandic Design Award **[Ap]**, which gives the business credibility and positive publicity **[An]**. This can attract environmentally conscious customers both in Iceland and internationally through its website, leading to increased sales and supporting growth **[An]**

However, having these social objectives could make it more difficult and expensive for AWG to grow **[K]**. Using natural materials and keeping waste to a minimum may cost more than using cheaper synthetic alternatives **[K]**. As AWG expands its product range and tries to reach more customers in other countries **[Ap]**, these higher production costs could reduce profit margins **[An]**, making it harder to fund further growth. The small workshop model using family and friends **[Ap]** may also be difficult to scale up **[An]**

Overall, AWG's social objectives have a largely positive impact on its plans to grow **[E]**. In today's market, more consumers are looking for sustainable and environmentally friendly products **[K]**, so AWG's values give it a strong competitive advantage that can drive online sales worldwide **[An]**. While costs may be higher, these social objectives are central to what makes AWG unique and attractive to customers **[E]**. Without them, AWG would lose the identity that sets it apart from larger, cheaper clothing businesses **[Ap]** and would struggle to compete on price alone

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> SunnySide Bakery is a small bakery in the town of Whitby, England. It was set up five years ago by Maria, who wanted to sell freshly baked bread and cakes using traditional recipes. The bakery has built a loyal customer base and employs three full-time staff. However, a new supermarket has recently opened nearby, offering cheaper baked goods.

Maria is reviewing the bakery's objectives and is considering two options:

- Option 1: Set a financial objective to reduce costs in order to lower prices and compete with the supermarket.
- Option 2: Set a non-financial objective to improve product quality and customer service to differentiate SunnySide from the supermarket.

Justify which one of these two options SunnySide Bakery should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
A business objective is a target or goal that a business sets out to achieve in order to guide its decisions and measure its success **[K]**

Reducing costs would allow Maria to lower her prices **[K]** and compete more directly with the new supermarket **[Ap]**. This could help SunnySide keep existing customers who might be tempted to switch to the supermarket for cheaper baked goods, protecting the bakery's revenue **[An]**

However, cutting costs could mean using cheaper ingredients or reducing staff hours **[K]**. This could lower the quality of SunnySide's traditional recipes and the level of customer service, which is what has built the bakery's loyal customer base over the past five years **[Ap]**. Maria could end up losing the very thing that makes her bakery special **[An]**

Improving product quality and customer service would help SunnySide stand out from the supermarket **[K]**. Customers who value freshly baked goods made with traditional recipes **[Ap]** are unlikely to find the same experience in a supermarket, so this objective could strengthen loyalty and attract new customers through word of mouth in Whitby **[An]**

The drawback is that improving quality and service may increase costs **[K]** for SunnySide. With only three staff and a small bakery **[Ap]**, Maria may struggle to fund improvements while the supermarket is already taking some of her customers, putting pressure on her income **[An]**

SunnySide should choose Option 2 **[E]**. A small bakery cannot realistically compete with a supermarket on price, so trying to cut costs would be a losing battle **[E]**. Instead, focusing on quality and service plays to SunnySide's strengths **[Ap]** and gives customers a clear reason to choose the bakery over the supermarket **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Even if Maria does not lower her prices significantly, spending less on areas such as packaging or energy bills means more  revenue is kept as profit → giving the bakery a stronger financial position to deal with the increased competition from the supermarket
> - The supermarket can buy ingredients in bulk at much lower prices due to economies of scale → it will always be able to undercut Maria, no matter how much she reduces costs → making this objective potentially unrealistic.
> - Focusing on quality and customer service → could allow Maria to charge premium prices to customers in Whitby who appreciate handmade, traditional baked goods → increase SunnySide's revenue and profit despite cheaper supermarket alternatives
> - Improving quality and service takes time to show results → in the short term, SunnySide may continue to lose customers to the supermarket while Maria invests in improvements

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> CoastLine Surf School is a small business based in Jeffreys Bay, South Africa. It was set up three years ago by Jake, a former professional surfer, and offers group and private surfing lessons to tourists and locals. The business employs six part-time instructors during the busy summer months. Jake has noticed that some customers have complained about long waiting times for lessons, and that two of his instructors have recently left to work for a rival surf school.

Jake is reviewing the business's non-financial objectives and is considering two options:

- Option 1: Set an objective to improve customer satisfaction by reducing waiting times and offering a better booking system.
- Option 2: Set an objective to improve employee retention by offering better pay and training to instructors.

Justify which one of these two options CoastLine Surf School should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
A non-financial objective is a business goal that is not directly related to making money, such as improving customer satisfaction or employee welfare **[K]**

Improving customer satisfaction by reducing waiting times would directly address the complaints **[Ap] **CoastLine has received. A better booking system would allow customers to plan their lessons in advance **[K]**, creating a smoother experience that could lead to positive reviews and word-of-mouth recommendations, helping to attract more tourists visiting Jeffreys Bay **[An]**

However, investing in a new booking system costs money **[K]**, and if Jake does not first solve the problem of losing instructors **[Ap]**, there may not be enough staff available to actually deliver more lessons. Reducing waiting times is difficult when the business is already short-staffed, meaning this objective may not be achievable in the short term **[An]**

Focusing on employee retention by offering better pay and training could stop more instructors from leaving to work for the rival surf school **[K] [Ap]**. Experienced, well-trained instructors would deliver higher quality lessons, which would naturally improve customer satisfaction and help build CoastLine's reputation in Jeffreys Bay **[An]**

The drawback is that increasing pay for six part-time instructors would raise CoastLine's costs **[K]**. As the business is seasonal and relies heavily on the busy summer months for income **[Ap]**, Jake may struggle to afford higher wages during quieter periods when fewer tourists are visiting **[An]**

CoastLine should choose Option 2 **[E]**. The root cause of the customer complaints is likely linked to losing instructors **[Ap]**, so retaining staff would solve both problems at once **[E]**. Focusing only on customer satisfaction without addressing staff retention would be a short-term fix, as CoastLine cannot deliver a good service without experienced instructors **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - If customers can easily book lessons online and receive a quick, reliable service, they are more likely to choose CoastLine over competitors → could help Jake increase his market share in the popular surfing destination of Jeffreys Bay
> - A better booking system does not address why customers are waiting in the first place → long waiting times are likely caused by having fewer instructors available since two have already left → a new booking system would simply show customers that there are no available slots
> - Offering training to instructors could also help CoastLine to offer a wider range of lessons → such as advanced courses or lessons for children → attract a broader range of customers → increasing revenue during the busy summer months
> - Better pay and training alone may not be enough to retain instructors → part-time and seasonal work means instructors may still leave for full-time roles for more job security →  instructors may leave anyway, wasting money that the business cannot easily afford to lose

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> BrightPath is a private tutoring company based in Manchester. It was founded by Amara eight years ago and employs twelve tutors. BrightPath provides one-to-one and small group tutoring sessions in maths and science to secondary school students. Over the past two years, demand for in-person tutoring has fallen by 25% as families increasingly choose cheaper online tutoring platforms. Amara has £40,000 in savings.

Amara is considering two options to improve the business's financial position:

- Option 1: Remain in the tertiary sector and reduce costs by moving all tutoring sessions online, cutting the expense of renting classroom space.
- Option 2: Move into the secondary sector alongside tertiary operations by producing and selling branded revision guides and workbooks, while continuing to offer tutoring services.

Justify which one of these two options BrightPath should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
The tertiary sector involves providing services to consumers and other businesses, such as tutoring. The secondary sector involves processing raw materials into finished products, such as manufacturing books **[K]**

Moving all tutoring online would reduce BrightPath's overhead costs **[K]**, as Amara would no longer need to pay rent for classroom space. This would help protect profit margins despite the 25% fall in demand for in-person tutoring **[Ap]**, without requiring Amara to develop entirely new skills or products **[An]**

However, switching entirely to online tutoring means BrightPath would be competing directly with the cheaper online platforms that are already taking its customers **[K]**. Without a clear unique selling point, BrightPath may struggle to differentiate itself in a crowded online market **[An]**. It also does not create any new revenue streams, so the business remains dependent on tutoring income alone **[Ap]**, meaning revenue may continue to decline if the trend towards cheaper alternatives continues **[An]**

Producing branded revision guides and workbooks would allow Amara to add value **[K]** by using the expertise of her twelve experienced tutors to create high-quality educational materials. These could be sold to students across the country, not just those in Manchester **[Ap]**, giving BrightPath access to a much larger market and reducing its dependence on local tutoring demand **[An]**

The drawback is that manufacturing and distributing physical products would require significant investment **[K]** from Amara's £40,000 savings **[Ap]**. If the guides do not sell well, Amara could lose most of her financial safety net, and her tutors are experienced in teaching, not writing or publishing, so developing quality materials would take time and additional resources **[An]**

BrightPath should choose Option 2 **[E]**. The decline in demand for in-person tutoring is driven by a long-term shift towards online learning, so simply cutting costs by going online is only a short-term fix that places BrightPath in direct competition with established, lower-cost platforms **[E]**. By producing its own revision guides and workbooks, BrightPath can leverage its tutors' subject expertise to create a unique product **[Ap]**, building a more diversified and sustainable business model for the future **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Remaining in the tertiary sector is less risky for Amara → she has eight years of experience running a tutoring business and understands the education market well
> - Moving online keeps the business focused on what Amara knows best → rather than moving into publishing where she has no experience and could make costly mistakes
> - Manchester has a large student population and strong demand for educational support → BrightPath's local reputation could be used to market revision guides effectively
> - Revision guides branded with BrightPath's name could build trust with parents who value expert-written materials → a unique selling point that generic online platforms would be unable to match

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Cresta is a small coffee farm in Colombia. It was set up fifteen years ago by Sofia Reyes and employs twelve workers who harvest coffee beans by hand. The beans are sold to large international companies who roast, package and sell them under their own brand names. Sofia has noticed that the price she receives for raw coffee beans has fallen steadily over the past three years, while the price of branded coffee in shops continues to rise.
> 
> Sofia has recently completed a course in coffee roasting and has saved \$40,000 from the business over the past five years. A roasting machine and packaging equipment would cost around \$35,000. Cresta has a strong reputation locally for producing high-quality beans, and Sofia has been approached by several independent cafés in Bogotá who are interested in buying locally roasted Colombian coffee.
> 
> Sofia is considering whether Cresta should move into the secondary sector by roasting and packaging its own coffee to sell directly to customers online.

Evaluate whether Cresta should move into the secondary sector by roasting and packaging its own coffee. You should use the information provided as well as your own knowledge of business.
parts.solutionMd:
The secondary sector involves turning raw materials into finished products through manufacturing or processing **[K]**

Moving into the secondary sector would allow Sofia to add value **[K]** to Cresta's coffee beans by roasting and packaging them. Instead of selling raw beans at falling prices to large companies **[Ap]**, she could charge much more for a finished product **[An]**. Sofia has already been approached by independent cafés in Bogotá, so there is existing demand, and with \$40,000 in savings and equipment costing \$35,000 **[Ap]**, she has enough finance to make the investment **[An]**

However, roasting and packaging coffee requires different skills and knowledge to farming **[K]**. Although Sofia has completed a roasting course, she has no experience of running a manufacturing operation, marketing a brand or selling online **[Ap]**. Her twelve workers are skilled at harvesting, not processing, so she may need to recruit or retrain staff, which would add further costs **[An]**. With only \$5,000 left after buying equipment **[Ap]**, Cresta would have very little financial cushion if things go wrong **[An]**

Overall, Cresta should move into the secondary sector **[E]**. The price of raw beans is falling while branded coffee prices are rising **[Ap]**, meaning staying in the primary sector alone will only lead to declining income. Sofia has the savings, the training and interested buyers already in place **[Ap]**, which reduces the risk **[E]**. She could manage the transition gradually by continuing to sell raw beans to international companies while building up the roasting side of the business, rather than switching completely and risking everything at once **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **12-mark 'evaluate' questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**

>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts linking points together to show clear cause and effect
>   - A clear, justified conclusion based on evaluation of the issues
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Cresta already has a strong local reputation for producing high-quality beans → gives Sofia a head start in building a brand
> - Customers and cafés are increasingly interested in knowing where their coffee comes from → being able to sell Colombian-roasted coffee directly from the farm could be a powerful selling point → larger international brands cannot easily match it
> - Sofia would be competing against large international companies that already have established brands, marketing budgets and distribution networks → as a small farm with no experience of selling online, Cresta may struggle to attract enough customers beyond the few cafés in Bogotá → difficult to generate enough sales to cover the cost of the equipment and justify the move

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Harvest is a lavender farm in the south of France. It was set up by Pierre twenty years ago and employs fifteen workers. Pierre sells his raw lavender to large cosmetics companies who use it to produce perfumes, soaps and essential oils. Over the past three years, the price Pierre receives for raw lavender has fallen by 20% due to cheaper imports from Eastern Europe. Pierre has €50,000 in savings.

Pierre is considering two options to improve the business's financial position:

- Option 1: Remain in the primary sector and reduce costs by investing in automated machinery to replace some manual labour.
- Option 2: Move into the secondary sector by building a small production unit to process lavender into essential oils and soaps, and sell them directly to tourists and local shops.

Justify which one of these two options Harvest should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
The primary sector involves extracting raw materials from the earth, such as farming. The secondary sector involves processing raw materials into finished products **[K]**

Investing in automated machinery would reduce Harvest's labour costs **[K]**, as machines can work faster and longer than manual workers. This would help Pierre maintain his profit margins despite the 20% fall in the price of raw lavender **[Ap]**, without having to change the way the business operates **[An]**

However, automation would mean some of Pierre's fifteen workers could lose their jobs **[K]**. This could damage Harvest's reputation in the local community **[An]**. It also does not solve the underlying problem of falling prices caused by cheaper imports from Eastern Europe **[Ap]**, meaning revenue may continue to decline even with lower costs **[An]**

Moving into the secondary sector by producing essential oils and soaps would allow Pierre to add value **[K] **to his lavender and sell finished products at much higher prices. Selling directly to tourists visiting the south of France **[Ap] **and local shops would give Harvest access to new customers and reduce its dependence on large cosmetics companies that are driving prices down **[An]**

The drawback is that building a production unit and learning new manufacturing processes would require significant investment **[K] **from Pierre's €50,000 savings **[Ap]**. If the products do not sell well, Pierre could lose most of his financial safety net, and his workers are experienced in farming, not manufacturing, so retraining would take time and money **[An]**

Harvest should choose Option 2 **[E]**. The falling price of raw lavender is unlikely to recover due to ongoing competition from Eastern Europe, so simply cutting costs is only a short-term fix **[E]**. By producing its own oils and soaps, Harvest can capture the added value that cosmetics companies currently take **[Ap]**, creating a more sustainable and profitable future for the business **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Staying in the primary sector is less risky for Pierre → he has twenty years of experience in lavender farming and understands the market well
> - Investing in machinery keeps the business focused on what Pierre knows best → rather than moving into manufacturing where he has no experience and could make costly mistakes
> - The south of France attracts millions of tourists each year → many of whom look for locally made products as souvenirs
> - Lavender oils and soaps with a "made on the farm" identity could command premium prices that mass-produced cosmetics cannot match → a unique selling point that cheaper Eastern European imports would be unable to compete with

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Stitch is a small tailoring business based in a busy high street in Milan, Italy. The owner, Luca, makes custom suits and dresses for local customers. Rent on the high street is €3,000 per month and continues to rise. Luca has noticed that several other shops on the high street have recently closed. However, his business relies heavily on taking customers' measurements in person and offering face-to-face consultations. A friend has suggested that Luca could save money by closing the shop and moving the business entirely online.

- Option 1: Remain on the high street in Milan.
- Option 2: Close the shop and operate entirely through e-commerce.

Justify which one of these two options Stitch should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
E-commerce is the buying and selling of goods or services over the internet. A high street location is a physical premises where customers can visit and purchase products in person **[K]**

Remaining on the high street means Luca can continue to offer face-to-face consultations and take measurements in person** [K]**. This is essential for a tailoring business where every suit and dress is custom made** [Ap]**, ensuring customers receive a high-quality, personalised service that could not easily be replicated online** [An]**

However, rent on the high street is €3,000 per month** [Ap]** and continues to rise **[K]**. With several other shops closing nearby, footfall may be declining, meaning Luca is paying more for a location that is attracting fewer potential customers, which could reduce his profit margins over time** [An]**

Moving entirely online would significantly reduce Stitch's fixed costs **[K]** by removing the €3,000 monthly rent **[Ap]**. This would allow Luca to keep more of his revenue as profit, giving the business greater financial security and the ability to invest in areas such as marketing to reach new customers** [An]**

The drawback is that selling online would make it very difficult for Luca to take customers' measurements in person **[K]**, which is a key part of his tailoring service** [Ap]**. Without face-to-face consultations, the quality and fit of his custom suits and dresses could suffer, leading to dissatisfied customers and a damaged reputation** [An]**

Stitch should choose Option 1 **[E]**. The nature of the business activity requires in-person contact with customers to take measurements and provide consultations** [Ap]**. Moving online would remove the core element of the service that makes Stitch successful, and while rent is expensive, the personal experience Luca offers justifies a high street presence that an online-only model cannot replace** [E]**

> - Operating online could allow Stitch to reach customers across Italy and beyond → expanding the market far beyond the local Milan area → increasing potential revenue without the limitation of a single physical location

- Option 2: Rent the larger garage on the outskirts and focus on growing online sales through a website.

Renting the town centre unit would put Kindle in a location with high footfall from both locals and tourists** [K]**. Queenstown is a popular tourist destination **[Ap]**, so visitors looking for locally made gifts like candles could provide a strong and steady source of revenue, especially during peak holiday seasons when tourist numbers are highest** [An]**

Renting the larger garage for NZ\$400 per month **[Ap]** would give Maia more production space at a much lower cost **[K]**. This would allow her to increase the volume of candles she produces and sell them through a website to customers across New Zealand, growing the business without being limited to only those who walk past a shop** [An]**

The drawback is that the garage has no passing trade**[Ap]**, meaning Maia would be entirely dependent on online sales to generate revenue **[K]**. Building an online customer base takes time and investment in a website and marketing, and without an established brand beyond the local weekend markets, sales could be slow to start** [An]**

Kindle should choose Option 2 **[E]**. The lower rent of NZ\$400 per month **[Ap] **protects Maia's savings and gives the business more financial security while it grows. The extra production space allows Maia to increase output, and selling online removes the limitation of relying solely on Queenstown footfall **[Ap]**, giving Kindle the potential to reach customers nationwide **[E]**. A town centre unit at NZ\$1,200 per month **[Ap] **is a significant risk for a small business that currently only sells at weekend markets** [E]**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Coral is a small diving school based on the coast of Zanzibar, Tanzania. It was set up eight years ago by Amina and employs six instructors. The business offers diving courses and snorkelling trips for tourists visiting the island. Coral has built a strong reputation through positive reviews on travel websites and word of mouth.
> 
> In recent years, Amina has noticed two significant changes. Rising sea temperatures have caused coral reef damage around Zanzibar, reducing the quality of the diving experience. At the same time, the growth of social media has made it easier for Coral to reach potential customers worldwide, and online bookings have increased by 40% over the past two years.

Evaluate the impact of external factors on Coral. You should use the information provided as well as your own knowledge of business.
parts.solutionMd:
External factors are forces outside of a business's control that can affect its decisions and performance** [K]**

The growth of social media has had a positive impact on Coral by making it easier to reach potential customers worldwide **[K]**. Online bookings have increased by 40% over the past two years** [Ap]**, which shows that this technological factor is helping Coral to attract more tourists to its diving courses and snorkelling trips. For a small business with six instructors based on an island** [Ap]**, social media provides a cost-effective way to market the business globally without the expense of traditional advertising** [An]**

However, rising sea temperatures causing coral reef damage is a serious environmental factor that threatens the core of Coral's business** [K]**. The quality of the diving experience around Zanzibar has been reduced** [Ap]**, meaning tourists may leave disappointed and post negative reviews on the travel websites where Coral has built its strong reputation **[Ap]**. If the reef continues to deteriorate, fewer tourists may choose to book diving courses or snorkelling trips, regardless of how effectively Amina uses social media to promote the business **[An]**

Overall, the environmental factor is likely to have a greater impact on Coral than the technological factor **[E]**. Social media and online bookings are helping the business to grow, but this growth depends entirely on Coral being able to offer a high-quality diving experience around Zanzibar's reefs** [Ap]**. If the reefs continue to decline, no amount of marketing will compensate for a product that no longer meets customer expectations. Amina may need to adapt by offering alternative experiences such as marine conservation trips **[Ap]** that turn the reef damage into an educational opportunity, rather than relying solely on traditional diving and snorkelling** [E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **12-mark 'evaluate' questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts linking points together to show clear cause and effect
>   - A clear, justified conclusion based on evaluation of the issues
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Positive reviews on travel websites have helped build Coral's reputation → but if reef damage leads to disappointing experiences, tourists may leave negative reviews instead → which could undo eight years of reputation building and reduce future bookings
> - Social media allows Coral to target specific groups of tourists interested in diving → this means Amina can spend less on marketing while reaching more potential customers worldwide → helping to keep costs low for a small business with only six instructors
> - Rising sea temperatures are beyond Amina's control and are unlikely to reverse quickly → meaning the quality of the diving experience may continue to decline → forcing Coral to either relocate to areas with healthier reefs or diversify into different tourist activities
> - The 40% increase in online bookings shows that demand for Coral's services is currently strong → this gives Amina a window of opportunity to save profits and invest in adapting the business → before the environmental damage becomes too severe to attract enough tourists

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Grove is a small olive oil producer based on the island of Crete, Greece. The owner, Nikos, employs 15 workers and sells bottled olive oil to supermarkets across Europe. Grove has won several awards for the quality of its oil.
> 
> In recent years, Nikos has faced two significant external challenges. Increasingly hot and dry summers caused by climate change have reduced olive harvests by 30% over the past three years. At the same time, a growing social trend towards plant-based diets and healthy cooking has increased demand for high-quality olive oil across Europe.

Nikos is considering two options to respond to these external factors:

- Option 1: Invest in irrigation technology to protect olive trees from drought and maintain harvest levels.
- Option 2: Use the increased demand to raise prices on the smaller quantity of oil produced, positioning Grove as a premium brand.

Justify which one of these two options Grove should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
An environmental factor is an issue relating to the natural world, such as climate change, that can affect how a business operates. A social factor is a change in society's attitudes or behaviour that can influence demand for a product **[K]**

Investing in irrigation technology would help protect Grove's olive trees from the increasingly hot and dry summers on Crete **[Ap]**. This would allow Nikos to maintain harvest levels and continue supplying the large volumes** [K] **of olive oil that European supermarkets require **[Ap]**, preventing the business from losing shelf space to competitors who can offer a more reliable supply** [An]**

However, irrigation technology is expensive to install and maintain** [K]**. With harvests already down by 30% over the past three years** [Ap]**, Grove's revenue is likely to have fallen, meaning Nikos may not have enough finance available to fund the investment without taking on debt** [An]**

Raising prices to position Grove as a premium brand would take advantage of the growing social trend towards healthy cooking and plant-based diets **[K]**. Since Grove has already won several awards for the quality of its oil **[Ap]**, customers may be willing to pay a higher price for an award-winning product, allowing Nikos to maintain or even increase revenue despite producing less oil **[An]**

The drawback is that European supermarkets typically compete on price **[K] **and may not be willing to stock a more expensive olive oil. Nikos currently sells to supermarkets across Europe **[Ap]**, and if they refuse to pay the higher price, Grove could lose its main sales channels and struggle to find enough alternative customers quickly** [An]**

Grove should choose Option 1** [E]**. The business relies on supplying large volumes of oil to European supermarkets** [Ap]**, and without reliable harvests this relationship is at risk. Investing in irrigation solves the root cause of the problem by protecting the olive trees from drought, securing Grove's long-term supply. While raising prices could work in the short term, it depends on supermarkets accepting higher costs, which is unlikely in a competitive market. Maintaining harvest levels gives Nikos the strongest foundation to keep supplying his existing customers while also benefiting from the growing demand for olive oil **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Irrigation would allow Grove to grow more consistently year on year → giving Nikos a reliable supply to offer European supermarkets → which builds trust and could lead to larger orders as demand for olive oil increases
> - The cost of irrigation may take years to pay back → during which time Grove is spending money while still dealing with reduced harvests on Crete → putting pressure on cash flow for a small business with 15 workers
> - A premium brand strategy requires no major upfront investment → Nikos can simply charge more for the oil he already produces → which would immediately improve profit margins without taking on financial risk
> - Supermarkets may replace Grove with a cheaper supplier if prices rise too much → once shelf space is lost it is very difficult to win back → meaning Grove could permanently lose its main route to customers across Europe

> BrightWave is a small solar panel manufacturer based in Manchester, UK. The owner, Verna, employs 20 workers and sells solar panels to construction firms and housing developers across the UK. BrightWave has built a strong reputation for producing reliable, high-efficiency panels.
> 
> In recent years, Verna has faced two significant external challenges. A sharp rise in interest rates has increased the cost of borrowing, making it more expensive for BrightWave's customers to finance large construction projects. At the same time, the UK government has introduced new legislation requiring all new-build homes to include renewable energy sources from 2026, significantly increasing future demand for solar panels.

Verna is considering two options to respond to these external factors:

- Option 1: Invest in expanding BrightWave's factory capacity now, using a bank loan, to be ready to meet the expected surge in demand when the new legislation takes effect in 2026.
- Option 2: Keep production at current levels and focus on securing long-term supply contracts with housing developers who will need solar panels to comply with the new legislation.

Justify which one of these two options BrightWave should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
An economic factor is an issue relating to the economy, such as interest rates, that can affect how a business operates. A political/legal factor is a change in government policy or law that can influence demand for a product **[K]**

Investing in expanding factory capacity would allow BrightWave to produce more solar panels in preparation for the expected increase in demand when the 2026 legislation takes effect **[Ap]**. Having greater capacity means Verna could fulfil large orders from housing developers **[K]** who will be legally required to install renewable energy sources in all new-build homes **[Ap]**, giving BrightWave a competitive advantage over rivals who may not be ready to supply at scale **[An]**

However, expanding using a bank loan when interest rates are high would significantly increase BrightWave's borrowing costs **[K]**. With customers already finding it more expensive to finance construction projects due to rising interest rates **[Ap]**, demand in the short term may be lower, meaning Verna could be repaying an expensive loan before the additional revenue from increased sales arrives in 2026 **[An]**

Securing long-term supply contracts with housing developers would guarantee future sales without requiring major upfront investment **[K]**. Since BrightWave already has a strong reputation for producing reliable, high-efficiency panels **[Ap]**, developers may prefer to lock in a trusted supplier now, giving Verna predictable revenue and reducing the risk of being undercut by competitors when the legislation comes into force **[An]**

The drawback is that without expanding capacity, BrightWave may not be able to fulfil the contracts it secures **[K]**. Verna currently employs only 20 workers and operates at existing production levels **[Ap]**, and if multiple developers place large orders at the same time, BrightWave could face production bottlenecks, leading to missed deadlines and potential damage to its reputation **[An]**

BrightWave should choose Option 2 **[E]**. The current high interest rate environment makes taking on a large bank loan a significant financial risk for a small business with 20 employees **[Ap]**. Securing long-term contracts first gives Verna guaranteed demand, which she could then use as evidence to negotiate better loan terms or attract investment when interest rates fall. This approach protects BrightWave's cash flow in the short term while still positioning the business to benefit from the 2026 legislation. Expanding capacity can follow once contracts are in place, reducing the risk of investing in growth before revenue is secured **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Expanding now means BrightWave would have capacity ready before competitors → allowing Verna to capture a larger share of the market when the 2026 legislation creates a surge in demand → which could establish BrightWave as a leading supplier in the sector
> - High interest rates may fall before 2026 → but Verna would already be locked into expensive loan repayments taken out at the current high rate → reducing profitability even when demand increases
> - Long-term contracts provide revenue certainty → Verna can plan production schedules and workforce needs in advance → reducing waste and improving efficiency for a small manufacturer
> - Developers may not honour contracts if economic conditions worsen → housing projects could be delayed or cancelled due to high borrowing costs → leaving BrightWave with committed resources but no orders to fulfil

> Soleil is a small vineyard in the south of France that produces wine and sells it to restaurants and shops across Europe. The French government has recently announced two changes that will affect businesses: a significant increase in corporation tax, and a major investment programme to upgrade the country's motorway network.

parts.solutionMd:
Government policy refers to the actions and decisions taken by a government that can affect how businesses operate **[K]**

The upgrade to the motorway network would directly benefit Soleil, as it transports all of its wine by road to customers in Germany, Spain and Italy **[Ap]**. Better roads would reduce delivery times that are currently being delayed by poor road conditions **[K]**, and could help to reverse the 15% rise in transport costs over the past two years, improving Soleil's profit margins and allowing it to offer a more reliable service to its restaurant and shop customers across Europe** [An]**

However, the significant increase in corporation tax means that Soleil will keep less of its profits** [K]**. For a small, family-run vineyard with 25 workers, this reduces the amount of money available to reinvest in the business **[Ap]**, which could limit Soleil's ability to maintain its vineyards, replace equipment or grow production at a time when costs have already been rising **[An]**

Overall, the impact on Soleil is mixed but the motorway investment is likely to be more beneficial in the long term **[E]**. Transport is central to Soleil's business model, as it relies on road deliveries to reach customers across three European countries** [Ap]**. Reduced delivery times and lower transport costs would provide ongoing savings year after year, whereas the corporation tax increase only applies to profits, which Soleil can manage by reinvesting more into the business before tax is calculated. The infrastructure improvement addresses the biggest operational challenge Soleil currently faces, making it the more significant of the two policy changes** [E]**

> - Improved motorways would not only benefit Soleil but also make it easier for competitors to transport their wine across Europe → meaning Soleil may not gain a competitive advantage from the infrastructure investment → as all wine producers using French roads would benefit equally
> - The family has run the vineyard for three generations and may have built up retained profit over the years → this financial cushion could help Soleil absorb the short-term impact of higher corporation tax → without needing to make immediate changes to prices or staffing levels

However, the government has announced an increase in interest rates, meaning the loan repayments will be higher than Yuki originally planned **[K]**. With only 12 workers and sales limited to local gift shops and restaurants **[Ap]**, Ember may not generate enough additional revenue to cover the higher repayments, which could create cash flow problems and put the business at risk **[An]**

Delaying the purchase and saving from retained profit means Yuki would avoid paying any interest at all **[K]**. This keeps Ember's costs low and protects the business from the financial pressure of higher loan repayments **[An]**, giving Yuki time to build up savings without risking the stability of a small business with 12 employees** [Ap]**

The drawback is that saving up over two years means Ember cannot increase its production capacity in the short term **[K]**. During this time, demand from gift shops and restaurants in Kyoto **[Ap]** may go unmet, and competitors could expand their own production and take customers that Yuki might otherwise have served** [An]**

Ember should choose Option 2 **[E]**. The increase in interest rates makes borrowing significantly more expensive, and for a small business with only 12 workers and a local customer base **[Ap]**, the risk of being unable to meet higher loan repayments is too great. Saving over two years is slower, but it protects the business from debt and ensures Yuki can buy the kiln without putting Ember's financial stability at risk **[E]**

> - Higher interest rates may also reduce consumer spending in Kyoto → meaning gift shops and restaurants may order less pottery from Ember → so taking on a loan at a time of falling demand could leave Yuki unable to meet repayments
> - Saving from retained profit gives Yuki full control over the business's finances → she would not owe money to a bank or be affected by any further interest rate increases → keeping the business independent and financially secure

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Terra is a fruit farm in rural Portugal that employs 40 seasonal workers to pick oranges and lemons. The owner, Miguel, exports most of his fruit to supermarkets in Germany and France. The Portuguese government has announced a 20% increase in the national minimum wage. At the same time, it has invested in upgrading the road network connecting rural areas to major ports.

Miguel is considering two options to manage the impact of these government policy changes:

- Option 1: Reduce the number of seasonal workers and invest in automated picking machinery to lower labour costs.
- Option 2: Keep all 40 workers and use the improved road network to expand into new export markets to increase revenue.

Justify which one of these two options Terra should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
Automation involves replacing manual labour with machinery to carry out tasks more efficiently **[K]**

Investing in automated picking machinery would reduce Terra's dependence on seasonal workers **[K]**, helping Miguel to control labour costs at a time when the minimum wage is increasing by 20% **[Ap]**, which would protect the farm's profit margins** [An]**

However, automated machinery is expensive to purchase and maintain **[K]**. Terra is a fruit farm that currently relies on 40 seasonal workers for picking, so Miguel would need significant investment to replace this labour **[Ap]**. If the machinery breaks down during harvest season, Terra could lose entire crops, which would be far more costly than paying higher wages **[An]**

Keeping all 40 workers and expanding into new export markets would allow Terra to increase its revenue to cover the higher wage costs** [K]**. The improved road network means Miguel can now transport fruit to major ports more quickly and cheaply, opening up opportunities to sell to supermarkets beyond Germany and France **[Ap] **and growing the customer base **[An]**

The drawback is that the 20% wage increase would immediately raise Terra's costs with no guarantee that new export markets will generate enough extra revenue to compensate **[K]**. Finding new supermarket customers in other countries takes time, and Miguel would be paying 40 workers higher wages **[Ap]** while waiting for these new markets to deliver returns, which could create cash flow problems in the short term** [An]**

Terra should choose Option 2 **[E]**. The improved road network is a significant opportunity that reduces transport costs and opens access to new markets. Reducing workers would limit Terra's picking capacity **[Ap]** and risk losing experienced seasonal staff who may not return in future years. By keeping all 40 workers and using the better infrastructure to grow revenue, Miguel addresses the higher wage costs through growth rather than cuts, which is a more sustainable strategy for the long-term future of the farm **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Fewer workers means Terra can operate with lower overheads even if the minimum wage rises further in the future → protecting the business from ongoing government policy changes → giving Miguel long-term cost certainty
> - Reducing the workforce could damage Terra's reputation in the local rural community → making it harder to recruit seasonal workers in future years if demand increases → leaving the farm short-staffed during busy harvest periods
> - Expanding into new export markets spreads Terra's risk across more countries → so if demand falls in Germany or France the business has other customers to rely on → making revenue more stable and predictable
> - New export markets may have different quality standards or regulations for imported fruit → meeting these requirements could be expensive and time-consuming for Miguel → delaying the revenue growth that Terra needs to cover the higher wage costs

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Most people recognise Heinz for the phrase ‘57 varieties’ even though it now produces many more than the original 57 varieties. H J Heinz, the founder of the Heinz business, believed the phrase sounded lucky.
> 
> *Kraft Heinz *is a world-wide producer of food products. It was formed from the merger of Kraft Foods and Heinz in 2015. This created the third largest food and drinks business in the USA and the fifth largest food and drinks business in the world.
> 
> *Kraft Heinz* has over 24 different brands, including Greenseas in Australia and Nutri+Plus in New Zealand. America has the largest number of brands from Maxwell House to Cool Whip. *Kraft Heinz* produces many different products including tomato sauce, ‘Mac&Cheese’, pasta and its famous baked beans that are used and eaten by many people.
> 
> *Kraft Heinz* uses many methods to advertise its products. These include posters, billboards and leaflets in supermarkets.
> 
> On 13 September 2022 the share price of Kraft Heinz in America at 10.00 am was \$36.55 and at 4.00 pm it was \$35.06.

Which **one** of the following is the percentage decrease in the share price?

Select **one** answer
parts.solutionMd:
**The correct answer is C** — 4.08%

The percentage decrease is calculated as:

$= \frac{36.55 - 35.06}{36.55} \times 100$

$= \frac{1.49}{36.55} \times 100$

$= 4.08 \%$

**A** is incorrect as 1.49 is simply the difference between $36 . 55 - 35 . 06$, not expressed as a percentage

**B** is incorrect as 1.96 results from dividing the sum of the two prices by 36.55 rather than the difference

**D** is incorrect as 4.25 results from dividing the difference by the closing price rather than the opening price:

$= \frac{1.49}{35.06} \times 100$

$= 4.25 \%$

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** advantage to a business of having limited liability.
parts.solutionMd:
The business exists as a separate legal entity to its owners **[1 mark]. **If the business goes into debt **[1 mark] **the business owners are protected from losing their personal assets **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award 1 mark for identifying an advantage to a business of having limited liability
> 
> 2 further marks are awarded for explaining the advantage, for a maximum of 3 marks
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - The business may raise large amounts of finance to expand **[1 mark] **through selling shares **[1 mark] a**s investors only risk losing the value of their shares if the business fails **[1 mark]**

>

The question asks you to explain **one** advantage, so pick one and expand on it in a chain of reasoning (point → cause/effect → consequence for the business). A common mistake is writing a definition of limited liability without linking it to an advantage — this will not earn any marks. Aim to write three connected sentences that build logically on each other to secure all 3 marks.
