parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> *IKEA* is a well-known home furniture retailer with stores throughout the world. It was started in 1943 by Ingvar Kamprad when he was given some money by his father for doing well at school. He wanted to produce furniture at a price that people could afford to buy.
> 
> He realised that transporting furniture to customers was difficult as goods were often damaged. He developed flat packs to avoid damage. A flat pack contained all the materials needed to self-assemble a table, a chair or a bed.
> 
> All *IKEA* stores are run as franchises.

Analyse the benefits to* IKEA* of all its stores being franchises
parts.solutionMd:
Franchisees will have local knowledge of the market in their country **[1 mark]**. This helps IKEA to offer products that suit local customers' tastes and needs **[1 mark]**, which could lead to higher sales of its affordable flat-pack furniture **[1 mark]**

Additionally, IKEA's brand and reputation are maintained by franchisees **[1 mark] **who follow its established business model. This means IKEA can ensure a consistent customer experience across its stores worldwide **[1 mark]**, helping to build customer loyalty and repeat purchases **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award up to 2 marks for identifying benefits to IKEA of all its stores being franchises
> 
> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for applying the benefits to IKEA's context
> 
> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for explaining the benefits to the business
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Franchisees pay IKEA a fee to operate under its brand name **[1 mark]**. This provides IKEA with a regular stream of income that can be used to invest in developing new products **[1 mark]**, such as improving its flat-pack furniture range **[1 mark]**
> - Franchisees are also responsible for the day-to-day running and costs of their own stores **[1 mark]**. This means IKEA can expand into new countries without taking on the financial risk itself **[1 mark]**, allowing it to grow quickly while keeping its own costs low **[1 mark]**
> - Accept any other appropriate response
> 
> Answers that list six benefits to IKEA of all its stores being franchises with no explanation will get a maximum of 1 mark
> 
> No marks are awarded for a definition alone

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a question asks you to "analyse", you need to do more than just state facts. Make sure you apply your knowledge to the specific business in the extract — in this case, IKEA and its flat pack furniture — and then develop your points by explaining the consequences or impact on the business. A good approach is to make a point, link it to the extract, and then explain why it matters for IKEA. For example, don't just say "franchisees pay fees" — go on to explain what this means for IKEA's revenue and success. Aim to write at least two or three well-developed points to access the full range of marks across both AO2 and AO3.

**[6 marks]**

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** benefit to a business that operates as a sole trader.

Think of it as a chain of reasoning: point → effect → further impact.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> The Alternative Drum School (TADS) was set up in the wealthy area of Cricklade, England in 2008 by Ollie Tanner who had a passion for and enjoyed drumming. Ollie invested all of his savings into the drumming school. He saw the potential of being located away from other drumming schools.
> 
> Ollie promotes his business by writing columns in local papers, performing at local music festivals and by word of mouth recommendations. He has invested heavily in computer technology to allow students to produce the music they enjoy playing.
> 
> Ollie finds it difficult to maintain a good work-life balance. Ollie currently works 60 hours a week in a business that does not have reliable profits.
> 
> At the moment *TADS* operates as a sole trader. As it becomes more successful Ollie is considering becoming a private limited company.

Evaluate whether *TADS* should consider becoming a private limited company. You should use the information provided as well as your own knowledge of business.
parts.solutionMd:
A private limited company is a business where ownership is divided into shares that can be sold privately to family, friends or investors, but not to the general public **[K]**

Becoming a private limited company would give Ollie the benefit of limited liability **[K]**. This means that if TADS fails, Ollie can only lose the money he has invested in the business, and his personal assets would be protected **[An]**. This is important because Ollie has already invested all of his savings into TADS **[Ap]**, and the business does not have reliable profits **[Ap]**, so there is a real risk he could lose everything if things go wrong. As a sole trader, Ollie has unlimited liability, which puts him in a very vulnerable position **[An]**. Also, by selling shares to investors, Ollie could raise additional finance  **[K] **to grow the business further, such as investing in more computer technology **[Ap]**

However, becoming a private limited company means Ollie would have to share ownership and decision-making with other shareholders **[K]**, which means he could lose some control over how TADS is run **[An]**. Since Ollie set up the business because of his passion for drumming **[Ap]**, having others influence decisions may take the business in a direction he does not want **[An]**. Setting up a private limited company also involves legal costs and paperwork **[K]**, which could be difficult for a small business with unreliable profits  **[Ap]** **[An]**

Overall, TADS should become a private limited company **[E]**. Remaining as a sole trader leaves Ollie exposed to unlimited liability, meaning he could lose his personal possessions if the business fails. He is also working 60 hours a week with unreliable profits **[Ap] **and no way to bring in extra finance, which is not sustainable **[E]**. While becoming a private limited company means sharing some control, Ollie could keep a majority of the shares to protect his vision for TADS while gaining limited liability and access to new investment that could help stabilise and grow the business **[E]**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Smile Dental Practice is a small dental clinic in Lisbon, Portugal. It was set up two years ago by Dr Amara Osei as a sole trader. The business has grown steadily thanks to positive online reviews and word-of-mouth recommendations from satisfied patients. It now has a waiting list of over 50 patients. Amara is struggling to manage the workload alone and often works late into the evening, which is affecting her work-life balance. She wants to bring in another dentist to help the business grow.

Amara is considering two options for changing the structure of the business:

- Option 1: Form a partnership with another qualified dentist
- Option 2: Establish a private limited company and sell shares to raise finance for expansion

Justify which one of these two options Smile Dental Practice should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
A partnership is a business owned by two or more people who share responsibility for running the business **[K]**. A private limited company is a business whose shares can be sold privately to raise finance and whose owners benefit from limited liability **[K]**

Forming a partnership with another dentist would allow Amara to share the workload **[K]** immediately. This would help reduce her long working hours **[Ap] **and improve her work-life balance while also allowing Smile to see more of the 50 patients currently on the waiting list, increasing revenue **[An]**

However, in a partnership, Amara would have to share the profits **[K]** with the new dentist **[Ap]**. She would also still have unlimited liability **[K]**, meaning her personal assets could be at risk if the business ran into debt. Additionally, Amara and her partner may disagree on how to run the practice, which could slow down decision-making **[An]**

Establishing a private limited company would give Amara limited liability, protecting her personal assets if the business were to fail **[K]**. Selling shares could also raise enough finance to hire additional staff, buy new equipment and expand the clinic **[Ap]**, allowing Smile to grow beyond what a simple partnership could achieve **[An]**

The drawback is that setting up a private limited company involves legal costs and paperwork **[K]**, which takes time and money. Amara would also have to share ownership with shareholders, and the process of establishing the company would not immediately solve her workload problem or reduce the waiting list **[Ap] [An]**

Smile should choose Option 1 **[E]**. Amara's most urgent problem is her heavy workload and poor work-life balance **[Ap]**, and a partnership would solve this straight away by bringing in another qualified dentist **[E]**. Becoming a private limited company would take time to set up and would not directly address the immediate need for another dentist to help with the growing patient waiting list **[E]**

> - Finding the right partner is risky → if the new dentist does not match Amara's standards, it could lead to poor patient experiences → damaging the strong reputation Smile has built through positive reviews over the past two years

> Pulse is a small chain of three fitness studios based in Tenerife, Spain. It was founded in 2018 by Elena Vargas, a former personal trainer, who used her savings and a bank loan to set up the business. Pulse offers high-intensity group classes and personal training sessions using a unique training method that Elena developed herself. The studios have become popular through social media and positive customer reviews, and Elena has built up €120,000 in retained profit over the past three years.
> 
> Elena personally trains all new instructors to make sure they deliver classes to her standard. She believes the quality of instruction is what sets Pulse apart from other gyms in Tenerife. Each studio is designed with the same layout, colour scheme and branding.
> 
> Elena wants to expand Pulse across mainland Spain and into other European countries. However, opening new studios requires significant investment in equipment, premises and staff training. Elena is considering whether to sell franchises as a way to grow the business.

Evaluate whether Pulse should sell franchises to expand the business. You should use the information provided as well as your own knowledge of business.
parts.solutionMd:
A franchise is where a business allows another operator to trade under its name in exchange for a fee **[K]**

Selling franchises would allow Pulse to expand across mainland Spain and into Europe without Elena having to fund each new studio herself **[K]**. Franchisees would pay for their own premises, equipment and staff, meaning Pulse can grow quickly while Elena keeps her €120,000 in retained profit **[Ap] **as a financial safety net rather than spending it all on expansion **[An]**

However, Elena currently trains all new instructors personally to maintain quality, which is what she believes sets Pulse apart **[Ap]**. If franchisees are responsible for running their own studios, Elena may not be able to oversee training at every location **[K]**. This could lead to inconsistent quality of instruction, which might damage the reputation that Pulse has built through positive reviews and social media **[An]**

Overall, Pulse should not sell franchises at this stage **[E]**. Elena's hands-on approach to training and her unique method  **[Ap] **are the core reasons for the business's success, and these would be very difficult to maintain across multiple franchise locations in different countries **[E]**. Instead, Elena could use her retained profit to open one or two new studios herself on the mainland, keeping full control over the quality of instruction and the consistent branding  **[Ap] **that makes Pulse distinctive **[E]**. Franchising could be reconsidered in the future once Pulse has established a proven system for training instructors without Elena's direct involvement **[E]**

$\text{Market growth} = \frac{\text{New market size}-\text{Old market size}}{\text{Old market size}} \times 100$

**[1 mark]**

`\text{Market growth} = \frac{180\,000\,000 - 150\,000\,000}{150\,000\,000} \times 100 = \frac{30\,000\,000}{150\,000\,000} \times 100 = \text{20}\%`

**20%** **[1 mark]**

> - 1 mark for the correct final answer
> - If the final answer is incorrect, award marks for correct working shown

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember that market growth measures the percentage change in the total size of a market over a period of time. Make sure you use the old (previous year) market size as the denominator — a common mistake is to divide by the new market size instead. Always show your working clearly so that even if your final answer is wrong, you can still pick up a method mark.

parts.solutionMd:
$\text{Flux's revenue} = ( 12 , 000 \times 45 ) + ( 8 , 500 \times 60 ) = 540 , 000 + 510 , 000 = \text{EUR}  1 , 050 , 000$

It has recently expanded by opening the first *Premier Inn *in Germany and has plans to open more in other countries. Evaluate whether a business such as *Premier Inn* should only consider profit to measure its success. You should use the information provided as well as your own knowledge of business.
parts.solutionMd:
Profit is the amount of money a business has left from its revenue after all costs have been deducted **[K]**

Profit is an important measure of success for Premier Inn because it shows whether the business is earning more than it is spending** [K]**. With over 820 hotels across the UK, UAE, India and Germany** [Ap]**, Premier Inn has very high operating costs, including staff wages, maintenance and restaurant supplies. If the business is making a profit, it means these costs are being covered and there is money left over to fund further expansion into new countries** [An]**

However, only considering profit could give Premier Inn an incomplete picture of its success **[K]**. For example, customer satisfaction is also important because Premier Inn relies on guests returning and recommending its hotels to others** [An]**. If profit is high but customer satisfaction is falling, this could indicate that Premier Inn is cutting costs in areas that affect the guest experience** [K]**, such as the quality of its restaurant meals or room maintenance across its 83,000 rooms** [Ap]**. This would eventually lead to fewer bookings and lower profit in the future** [An]**

Overall, Premier Inn should not only consider profit to measure its success **[E]**. While profit is essential for funding its expansion into countries like Germany and beyond **[Ap]**, Premier Inn should also monitor measures such as customer satisfaction and employee satisfaction to ensure long-term success. A business with 820 hotels and restaurants **[Ap] **depends on consistent service quality, and measures beyond profit help to identify problems before they affect the bottom line. Profit tells Premier Inn how it has performed in the past, but other measures help to predict how it will perform in the future** [E]**

> - Employee satisfaction is another important measure for a business with over 820 hotels → unhappy staff may provide poor service to guests in the hotels and restaurants → which would damage Premier Inn's reputation and reduce bookings even if current profit figures look healthy
> - Premier Inn's current ratio could be calculated from its 2022 figures (£9,566m ÷ £5,447m = 1.76) → this shows the business can comfortably pay its short-term debts → which is an important measure of financial health that profit alone does not reveal
> - Revenue growth could also be used to measure success → if Premier Inn's revenue is increasing as it opens hotels in Germany and other countries → this shows the business is expanding successfully even if profit temporarily dips due to the costs of opening new locations

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Thrive is a small gym in Barcelona, Spain. It was set up four years ago by Marta and has grown to employ eight personal trainers. The gym has 600 members and revenue has increased every year since it opened. However, Marta has noticed that several members have recently cancelled their memberships, and online reviews suggest that some customers are unhappy with the cleanliness of the facilities and long waiting times for equipment.

Marta wants to choose the best way to measure the success of Thrive going forward. She is considering two options:

- Option 1: Focus on financial measures of success, such as revenue and profit.
- Option 2: Focus on non-financial measures of success, such as customer satisfaction and employee satisfaction.

Justify which one of these two options Thrive should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
Revenue is the total income a business receives from selling its goods or services [K]. Customer satisfaction is a measure of how well a business meets the expectations of its customers **[K]**

Focusing on financial measures such as revenue and profit would give Marta a clear picture of whether Thrive is making enough money to survive and grow **[K]**. Revenue has increased every year since the gym opened **[Ap]**, so tracking this would show whether the business continues to grow financially and can afford to pay its eight personal trainers and cover running costs** [An]**

However, Thrive's revenue may be hiding a deeper problem** [K]**. Several members have recently cancelled their memberships, and online reviews mention poor cleanliness and long waiting times for equipment** [Ap]**. If Marta only looks at revenue, she may not notice that the business is losing customers until it is too late and income starts to fall sharply** [An]**

Focusing on non-financial measures such as customer satisfaction would allow Marta to identify and address the problems highlighted in the online reviews **[K]**. By acting on feedback about cleanliness and waiting times at the Barcelona gym **[Ap]**, Marta could improve the experience for existing members, reducing cancellations and encouraging positive reviews that attract new customers** [An]**

The drawback is that non-financial measures are harder to track and can be subjective** [K]**. Online reviews from a small number of Thrive's 600 members **[Ap]** may not represent the views of the whole membership, meaning Marta could invest time and money fixing issues that only affect a minority of customers** [An]**

Thrive should choose Option 2 **[E]**. The cancellations and negative online reviews **[Ap]** are warning signs that cannot be seen in the revenue figures alone. If Marta does not address customer satisfaction now, more members will leave and revenue will eventually fall. Non-financial measures act as an early warning system, allowing Marta to fix problems before they damage Thrive's finances. Focusing only on revenue and profit would give a misleadingly positive picture while the business is actually losing the loyal members it depends on **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Profit is essential for any business to survive → if Thrive is not profitable Marta cannot afford to pay her eight trainers or maintain the gym facilities → which would make the cleanliness and equipment problems even worse
> - Employee satisfaction could also be measured under Option 2 → if Thrive's personal trainers are unhappy they may deliver a poorer service to the 600 members → leading to further cancellations and negative reviews
> - Revenue growth does not show whether individual members are spending more or whether new members are simply replacing those who leave → Marta could believe the business is growing while actually churning through customers → which is unsustainable in the long term
> - Improving customer satisfaction often requires spending money on better facilities and more equipment → this would reduce Thrive's profit in the short term → meaning Marta needs to balance both financial and non-financial measures rather than relying on one alone

An automated text message system would directly address the customer complaints about not being informed when prescriptions are ready for collection** [K]**. The drawback is that an automated system does not fix the internal problem of medication regulation updates not reaching all staff** [K]**. If employees across the three pharmacies continue to make errors because they are not receiving important information** [Ap]**, this could lead to serious consequences for customers' health that would be far more damaging to Beacon than late prescription notifications **[An]**

Beacon should choose Option 1 **[E]**. Errors caused by staff not receiving medication regulation updates could have serious health consequences for customers across all three Dublin pharmacies** [Ap]**. *Irsi Chocolatier* is a business with three loyal employees. As it expands it wants to ensure its current and new employees remain happy and motivated within the workplace.

Evaluate the impact of *Irsi Chocolatier* using financial methods of motivation on its employees. You should use the information provided as well as your own knowledge of business.
parts.solutionMd:
Financial methods of motivation include pay rises, bonuses and commission, which reward employees with increased earnings in return for their performance or loyalty** [K]**

Financial rewards such as bonuses could motivate Irsi's employees to produce higher quality handmade chocolates and deliver better customer service **[K]**, which is important for a business operating in a highly competitive area of Brussels with many other chocolate shops nearby **[Ap]**. However, Irsi is a small family business with only three employees and four directors **[Ap]**, meaning its financial resources are likely to be limited, and it may struggle to sustain meaningful pay rises or bonuses over the long term **[K][An]**. According to Herzberg's theory, pay is a hygiene factor rather than a true motivator **[K]**, suggesting that while financial rewards may prevent dissatisfaction, they may not be sufficient to keep Irsi's employees genuinely motivated **[An]**. Non-financial methods such as recognition, greater responsibility or flexible working may be more effective for a small, close-knit team** [E]**

parts.solutionMd:

One benefit of job enrichment is that it gives IKEA's factory workers greater variety and responsibility in their roles** [K] **constructing flat pack furniture**, **which according to Maslow addresses higher-level esteem needs and increases employees' sense of achievement and commitment to the business** [An]**

However, with 2,500 workers spread across 30 sites **[Ap]**, a wide span of control would mean each manager supervises a much larger number of employees **[K]**, making it extremely difficult to monitor safety standards and quality of work on complex construction projects **[An]**. In an industry where errors can have serious consequences, close supervision is essential and a taller structure with narrower spans of control is more appropriate **[E]**

Overall, while a flatter structure could reduce costs for Pillar **[E]**, the safety-critical nature of construction work across 30 sites **[Ap]** means close supervision at every level is essential **[An]**. > **[case-study]**
> Vesta is a UK estate agency founded in 2008. It now has 55 branches across England and Wales, each employing a team of sales negotiators, valuers and administrative staff who work with buyers, sellers and landlords in their local area.Branch managers have strong local knowledge and well-established relationships with clients in their communities.
> 
> Vesta has grown quickly in recent years, and its directors are finding it increasingly difficult to make all key decisions from head office while also planning for future growth. Vesta is planning to open a further 15 branches over the next two years.

Vesta is considering how best to structure decision-making across the business. It is considering two options:

- Option 1: centralised decision-making — all key decisions are made by Vesta's directors at head office
- Option 2: decentralised decision-making — branch managers are given the authority to make key decisions for their own branch

Justify which one of these two options Vesta should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
Centralised decision-making means all key decisions are made by senior managers at the top of the organisation, while decentralised decision-making  gives authority to managers at a lower level to make decisions for their own area of the business **[K] **

One benefit of centralised decision-making is that Vesta's directors can ensure consistent standards and policies are applied across all 55 branches **[Ap]**, reducing the risk of individual branches making decisions that damage the business's reputation or brand **[K] [An]**

However, with directors already finding it difficult to manage decision-making across 55 branches** [Ap]**, centralising all key decisions as Vesta grows to 70 branches would place even greater pressure on head office **[K]**, slowing down decision-making and potentially causing the business to miss opportunities in fast-moving local property markets** [An]**

One benefit of decentralised decision-making is that Vesta's branch managers can use their strong local knowledge and established client relationships to make faster and better-informed decisions **[Ap][K]**, responding quickly to changes in local property markets without waiting for approval from head office** [An]**

However, giving branch managers full decision-making authority carries the risk that decisions may be inconsistent across Vesta's branches** [K]**, potentially leading to variations in the quality of service offered to buyers, sellers and landlords in different areas **[Ap] [An]**

Vesta should choose decentralised decision-making** [E]**. As a business with 55 branches across England and Wales and plans to grow further** [Ap]**, it is no longer practical for directors to manage all decisions centrally** [An]**. Branch managers' local expertise and client relationships mean they are best placed to make timely decisions that reflect the needs of their local market, making decentralisation the more effective and sustainable approach as Vesta continues to expand **[E]**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> The first *Premier Inn *hotel was opened in 1987. *Premier Inn *now has over 820 hotels in the UK, United Arab Emirates (UAE) and India with over 83,000 rooms. It has recently expanded by opening the first* Premier Inn* in Germany and has plans to open more in other countries.
> 
> The majority of the hotels have restaurants with facilities for guests to buy meals and drinks.
> 
> *Premier Inn* wants to retain its employees so it can continue to maintain the service it provides for guests.

*Premier Inn* has employees across the world. When a new position becomes available, *Premier Inn* must make sure that the recruitment method used is the correct one for the vacant position. It is considering the following two options:

** Option 1: ** internal recruitment from within *Premier Inn *hotels around the world

**Option 2:** external recruitment, by using an employment agency

Justify which **one **of these two options *Premier Inn* should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
Recruitment is the process of finding and attracting suitable candidates to fill a job vacancy **[K]**. Internal recruitment means Premier Inn would fill the position with an existing employee from one of its 820 hotels worldwide **[Ap]**. This is beneficial because the employee will already understand how Premier Inn operates and the standard of service expected, meaning less training is needed and they can settle into the role quickly **[An]**

However, internal recruitment creates another vacancy that still needs to be filled **[K]**. With hotels across the UK, UAE, India and Germany**[Ap]**, moving staff between locations could also be costly and disruptive, and it does not bring any fresh  ideas or new skills into the business **[An]**

External recruitment through an employment agency would give Premier Inn access to a much wider pool of candidates **[K]** with different skills and experience. This could be especially useful as Premier Inn expands into new countries like Germany**[Ap]**, where local candidates may better understand the culture and language of the market **[An]**

On the other hand, using an employment agency can be expensive **[K]**, as agencies charge fees for finding candidates. External recruits will also need more training to learn how Premier Inn operates, which takes time and could temporarily affect the quality of service provided to hotel guests **[Ap] [An]**

Premier Inn should choose Option 1, internal recruitment **[E]**. Since Premier Inn wants to retain its employees **[Ap]**, promoting from within rewards loyalty and motivates staff to stay with the company. External recruitment through an agency is costly and risky when maintaining consistent service standards across a growing global business is the priority **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Internal candidates already know Premier Inn's culture → less disruption to existing teams → helping Premier Inn maintain the service standards that guests expect
> - Employment agency brings in candidates with local knowledge of new markets like Germany → helps Premier Inn adapt its service to new countries → supporting its international expansion plans
> - Internal promotion signals to all Premier Inn staff that hard work is rewarded → increases motivation across the workforce → helping Premier Inn retain more employees and reduce recruitment costs long term
> - Agency fees and training costs for external candidates are high → this reduces Premier Inn's profit margins → making internal recruitment the more financially sensible option for an established business

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Most people recognise Heinz for the phrase ‘57 varieties’ even though it now produces many more than the original 57 varieties. H J Heinz, the founder of the Heinz business, believed the phrase sounded lucky.
> 
> Kraft Heinz is a worldwide producer of food products. It was formed from the merger of Kraft Foods and Heinz in 2015. This created the third-largest food and drinks business in the USA and the fifth-largest food and drinks business in the world. Kraft Heinz has over 24 different brands, including Greenseas in Australia and Nutri+Plus in New Zealand. America has the largest number of brands, from Maxwell House to Cool Whip. Kraft Heinz produces many different products, including tomato sauce, ‘Mac&Cheese’, pasta and its famous baked beans that are used and eaten by many people.
> 
> Kraft Heinz uses many methods to advertise its products. These include posters, billboards and leaflets in supermarkets.

*Kraft Heinz* will need to recruit more managers to take responsibility for new production lines. It is considering two options:

**Option 1:** promote existing employees

**Option 2:** advertise managerial positions externally.

Justify which **one **of these two options* Kraft Heinz* should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
Internal recruitment means promoting existing employees to fill a vacancy, while external recruitment involves advertising a position outside the business to attract new candidates** [K]**

One benefit of promoting existing employees is that they already understand Kraft Heinz's production processes and brand standards **[K]** for the wide range of food products it manufactures **[Ap]**, meaning they would need less time and training before being able to manage a new production line effectively **[An]**

However, a drawback is that Kraft Heinz may not have existing employees with the managerial experience needed **[K] **to oversee its complex new production lines **[Ap]** which could mean appointing a manager who is not fully equipped for the role, leading to poor performance and inefficiency on the new lines** [An]**

One benefit of advertising externally is that it gives Kraft Heinz access to a wider pool of candidates **[K]**, including experienced managers from other large food and drink businesses **[Ap]** who could bring fresh expertise to Kraft Heinz's new production lines. This increases the chance of finding a highly skilled manager who can lead the new lines effectively from the start **[An]**

However, external candidates would be unfamiliar with Kraft Heinz's specific products and processes [K], meaning significant time and money would need to be invested in training on operating, for example, soup production lines **[Ap]** confidently, potentially delaying output **[An]**

Kraft Heinz should choose Option 1: promote existing employees **[E]**. As the fifth-largest food and drinks business in the world with over 24 brands **[Ap]**, Kraft Heinz's production processes are complex and highly specific, meaning an internal candidate's existing knowledge would allow them to manage a new production line far more quickly than an external hire** [E]**. External recruitment would be costly and time-consuming, making internal promotion the more efficient and practical choice** [E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Existing Kraft Heinz employees already know the business's brands and products → they can take on managerial responsibility more quickly → helping new production lines to run efficiently from the start
> - External candidates may bring specialist management experience from other large food businesses → introducing new methods that improve productivity → helping Kraft Heinz maintain its position as the fifth-largest food and drinks business in the world
> - Promoting internally motivates other Kraft Heinz employees by showing that progression is possible → increasing staff loyalty and reducing turnover → lowering long-term recruitment costs for the business
> - External advertising reaches a larger pool of candidates → increasing the chance of finding a highly skilled manager  → which could lead to better performance on the new production lines

However, providing off-the-job training for all 8,000 employees would be extremely costly** [K]**, and with Grove keeping costs tightly controlled in order to pass savings on to customers** [Ap]**, this level of expenditure could force prices to rise and undermine Grove's competitive position in the market **[An]**. Furthermore, Grove's high rate of staff turnover among checkout and warehouse teams** [Ap]** means the business could repeatedly pay for off-the-job training for employees who leave quickly, making it a poor use of limited resources** [An]**

Overall, off-the-job training is most valuable for Grove's department managers and specialist food counter staff** [E]**, where qualifications and leadership skills are essential **[K]**. For the majority of roles, such as checkout operators and warehouse workers** [Ap]**, on-the-job training is more cost-effective and directly relevant to their day-to-day duties. Applying off-the-job training to all employees would place too great a strain on Grove's finances and contradict its commitment to keeping costs low** [E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts linking points together to show clear cause and effect
>   - A clear, justified conclusion based on evaluation of the issues
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**

> - Off-the-job training removes Grove's employees from stores during their training period → reducing staffing levels across 95 locations → which could negatively affect customer service at a time when Grove is already stretched by opening 15 new stores
> - Department managers could benefit from specialist off-the-job management training → improving leadership skills across the business → helping Grove maintain consistent standards as it expands
> - Grove's high staff turnover means repeatedly funding off-the-job training for checkout and warehouse staff → increasing costs significantly → making on-the-job training a far more financially sensible option for these roles
> - Providing food hygiene qualifications through off-the-job training for fresh food and deli staff ensures Grove complies with strict food hygiene regulations → protecting the business from legal penalties → which is critical for maintaining Grove's reputation and keeping customers loyal in a highly competitive market

parts.solutionMd:

Which **one **of the following is the markup on a pack of balloons?

Select **one **answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**The correct answer is D**

Markup is calculated as:

$\text{Markup} = \frac{\text{Selling price}-\text{Cost price}}{\text{Cost price}} \times 100$

$\text{Markup} = \frac{16.90-7.20}{7.20} \times 100$

$\text{Markup} = \frac{9.70}{7.20} \times 100$

`\text{Markup} = 134.72\,\%`

**A** is incorrect as 7.20 % corresponds to the cost of the balloon pack, not the markup

**B** is incorrect as 9.70 % corresponds to the profit on the balloon pack in SGD, not the markup percentage

**C** is incorrect as 69.84 % is the result of dividing the profit by the selling price (margin), not the cost price (markup)

Markup is calculated as the difference between the selling price and the cost, expressed as a percentage of the cost:

> Most people recognise Heinz for the phrase ‘57 varieties’ even though it now produces many more than the original 57 varieties. H J Heinz, the founder of the Heinz business, believed the phrase sounded lucky.
> 
> *Kraft Heinz* is a world-wide producer of food products. It was formed from the merger of Kraft Foods and Heinz in 2015. This created the third largest food and drinks business in the USA and the fifth largest food and drinks business in the world.
> 
> *Kraft Heinz* has over 24 different brands, including Greenseas in Australia and Nutri+Plus in New Zealand. America has the largest number of brands from Maxwell House to Cool Whip. *Kraft Heinz* produces many different products including tomato sauce, ‘Mac&Cheese’, pasta and its famous baked beans that are used and eaten by many people.
> 
> *Kraft Heinz* uses many methods to advertise its products. These include posters, billboards and leaflets in supermarkets.

*Kraft Heinz* has factories in over 29 countries. Countries include Japan, The Netherlands, New Zealand and America.

**Figure 3 **shows the gross profit for Kraft Heinz for the three months ending 25 June 2022:

|   | Million (US Dollars) |
|---|---|
| Gross profit | 1 984 |
| Revenue | 6 554 |

**Figure 3**

Calculate, to two decimal places, the gross profit margin for *Kraft Heinz* for the three months ending 25 June 2022. You are advised to show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
$\text{Gross profit margin} = \frac{\text{Gross profit}}{\text{Revenue}} \times 100$

$= \frac{1984}{6554} \times 100$ **[1 mark]**

= **30.27%** **[1 mark]**

> Award 1 mark for the correct final answer of **30.27%**.

parts.solutionMd:
The acid test ratio shows TBTS's ability to meet its short-term debts without relying on selling its toy stock **[1 mark]**. The improvement from 0.75 in 2018 to 0.88 in 2020 suggests that TBTS's liquidity position is strengthening over time **[1 mark]**, helping managers assess whether the business is becoming better placed to meet its short-term financial obligations across its three Singapore shops **[1 mark]**

The acid test ratio is particularly useful for TBTS because, as a toy retailer, it holds significant amounts of stock that cannot always be quickly converted into cash **[1 mark]**. By excluding stock from the calculation, the acid test gives a more accurate picture of TBTS's true liquidity **[1 mark]**, helping managers assess whether the business has sufficient liquid assets to meet immediate obligations such as rent for its shopping mall and Jewel Changi Airport locations without needing to rely on toy sales **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for explaining the impact on TBTS's ability to manage its financial performance.
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer:**
> 
> - Although the acid test ratio has improved across all three years, TBTS's ratio remains below 1.0 in 2018, 2019 and 2020 **[1 mark]**, indicating that current liabilities exceed liquid assets throughout this period **[1 mark]**, suggesting that TBTS may still face challenges meeting all short-term debts without selling stock, which is useful information for managers planning cash flow across the three shops **[1 mark]**
> - The acid test ratio allows TBTS to compare its liquidity performance with previous years **[1 mark]**, helping managers identify whether the trend of improvement seen between 2018 and 2020 is sustainable **[1 mark]**, and informing decisions about whether to hold larger cash reserves or seek additional finance to improve liquidity further **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> The *LEGO *Group is a privately-owned business in Denmark. The business was founded in 1932 by the Kristiansen family. The family still owns it. The name *LEGO *is an abbreviation of two Danish words, ‘leg godt’ which means ‘play well’. It is now one of the world’s largest manufacturers of toys with 15 factories and over 18,000 employees around the world.
> 
> *LEGO* manufactures toys, games and art materials for boys and girls of all ages, and products from films such as Star Wars and Harry Potter. It believes that children are the role models of the future and playing with *LEGO* can support children in a developing and complex world.

*LEGO *sells pineapple pencil holders for 148.00 DKK. The markup is 15%.

Calculate, to two decimal places, the cost of making the pineapple pencil holders. You are advised to show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
**Method 1:**

$148 \times 0 . 85$ **[1 mark]**

$= 125 . 80$ **[1 mark]**

**Method 2:**

$148 \times 0 . 15 = 22 . 20$ **[1 mark]**

$148 - 22 . 20 = 125 . 80$ **[1 mark]**

Final answer: **125.80 DKK**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award 1 mark for correctly substituting numbers into the formula.
> 
> Award 1 mark for the correct final answer.
> 
> Award full marks for the correct numerical answer without working.
> 
> Either method is acceptable for full marks.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many students confuse markup with margin. A markup of 15% means the cost is increased by 15% to arrive at the selling price. To reverse this, you can multiply the selling price by 0.85 (i.e. `100\% - 15\% = 85\%`) to find the cost. Always show your working clearly — even if you get the final answer correct, showing your method ensures you can still pick up marks if you make a small arithmetic error.

**[2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Miru is a small retail shop in the Harajuku district of Tokyo, Japan, selling locally designed clothing and accessories. The business was founded four years ago by Keiko Tanaka, who designs some of the items sold in the shop herself. Miru employs two part-time assistants and has built a loyal customer base among young shoppers in the area.
> 
> As the business has grown, Keiko has started to review its financial performance more closely and is considering which accounting ratios would be most useful to help her assess how the business is performing.

Keiko is unsure about what she should prioritise when assessing Miru's financial performance.

- Option 1: Gross profit margin
- Option 2: Current ratio

Justify which one of these Keiko should prioritise.
parts.solutionMd:
The gross profit margin measures the proportion of revenue retained as gross profit after deducting cost of sales, while the current ratio compares current assets with current liabilities to assess a business's liquidity** [K]**

Calculating the gross profit margin would help Keiko assess whether Miru's prices generate sufficient profit after cost of sales **[K]**, identifying whether the locally designed clothing is priced effectively** [Ap]**, and informing decisions about whether prices or sourcing costs need to be adjusted **[An]**

However, the gross profit margin does not reveal Miru's ability to meet its short-term debts **[K]**, meaning Keiko could overlook liquidity problems despite a healthy profit margin **[Ap]**, leading to the shop struggling to pay suppliers even while appearing profitable **[An]**

Calculating the current ratio shows Keiko whether Miru has sufficient current assets to cover its current liabilities **[K]**, helping her assess whether the shop can meet short-term obligations such as supplier payments **[Ap]**, and reducing the risk of the business facing cash flow difficulties **[An]**

However, the current ratio does not measure Miru's profitability **[K]**, meaning Keiko could maintain strong liquidity while generating insufficient gross profit to sustain the business in the long term **[Ap]**, missing the opportunity to identify and address pricing or cost problems **[An]**

Keiko should prioritise the gross profit margin **[E]**. As a small retail clothing shop selling locally designed items **[Ap]**, ensuring pricing generates sufficient profit is the most pressing long-term concern, and liquidity can be monitored separately through careful cash flow management **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Volta is a family restaurant in Porto, Portugal, specialising in traditional Portuguese cuisine. The business was founded six years ago by Isabel Ferreira and her husband and seats forty customers. Volta employs eight members of staff and has built a strong reputation with both local residents and tourists visiting the city. However, over the past two years Isabel has noticed that the business's gross profit margin has been falling due to rising food costs.
> 
> She is now considering how to respond to improve the restaurant's financial performance.

Isabel is considering two options to improve Volta's gross profit margin.

- Option 1: Increase menu prices
- Option 2: Source cheaper ingredients to reduce the cost of sales

Justify which one of these options Isabel should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
The gross profit margin measures the proportion of revenue retained as gross profit after deducting cost of sales **[K]**. A falling gross profit margin indicates the business retains less profit from each unit of revenue it generates** [K]**

Increasing menu prices would raise Volta's revenue per meal** [K]**, widening the gap between revenue and cost of sales **[An]**, which would directly improve the gross profit margin and help Isabel restore the restaurant's profitability** [Ap]**

However, higher prices could reduce customer demand** [K]**, particularly as Porto has many competing restaurants** [Ap]**, meaning lower customer numbers could reduce total revenue and offset the benefit of the price increase** [An]**

Sourcing cheaper ingredients would reduce Volta's cost of sales** [K]**, lowering the proportion of revenue spent on food **[An]**, which would improve the gross profit margin without risking a fall in customer numbers **[Ap]**

However, cheaper ingredients could reduce the quality of Volta's dishes **[K]**, damaging the restaurant's reputation with loyal customers in Porto** [Ap]**, which could lead to a fall in revenue that outweighs the savings made on ingredient costs** [An]**

Isabel should choose to source cheaper ingredients **[E]**. Raising prices in a competitive restaurant market risks losing customers to rivals **[Ap]**, whereas finding more affordable suppliers could reduce the cost of sales while maintaining food quality if managed carefully **[E]**

>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer:**
> 
> - Increasing menu prices raises revenue per meal → widens the gap between revenue and cost of sales → gross profit margin improves → helps Isabel restore Volta's profitability without reducing ingredient quality
> - Higher prices risk reducing demand → Porto has many competing restaurants → lower customer numbers reduce total revenue → the improvement in gross profit margin may be offset by lost sales
> - Sourcing cheaper ingredients reduces cost of sales → lowers the proportion of revenue spent on food → gross profit margin improves directly → without risking a fall in the number of customers visiting Volta
> - Cheaper ingredients may reduce the quality of traditional Portuguese dishes → damages Volta's reputation with loyal local customers and tourists → could lead to falling revenue → outweighing the cost savings and worsening the gross profit margin further

parts.problemMd:

> Norva is an outdoor clothing and equipment business based in Bergen, Norway. Founded ten years ago by Erik Hansen, the business sells hiking and skiing gear through three stores across Norway and a growing online shop. The business is particularly busy during the winter ski season and the summer hiking season. Norva employs twenty-five staff across its stores and head office. Erik regularly reviews the business's financial documents and accounting ratios to assess performance and inform decisions about the future direction of the business.

Evaluate the view that accounting ratios are the most useful tool for Norva when making business decisions.
parts.solutionMd:
Accounting ratios are calculations based on financial data that help a business assess its financial performance** [K]**. They include profitability ratios such as the gross profit margin and liquidity ratios such as the current ratio **[K]**

Accounting ratios allow Norva to assess its financial performance using objective, quantifiable data **[K]**, such as calculating the gross profit margin across its three Norwegian stores to identify trends in profitability **[Ap]**, helping Erik pinpoint whether pricing or the cost of outdoor equipment needs to be addressed to improve financial performance **[An]**

However, accounting ratios are based on historical financial data and do not capture qualitative factors **[K]**. For a seasonal business selling outdoor clothing and equipment in Norway **[Ap]**, customer satisfaction and changing trends in hiking and skiing are equally important considerations, meaning ratios alone cannot inform decisions about which new product lines to introduce **[An]**. Market research would provide more relevant insights for these decisions **[E]**

Overall, accounting ratios are highly useful for assessing Norva's financial health and identifying specific problems such as falling profitability **[E]**. However, they should not be the only tool used **[E]**, as qualitative information about customer preferences and seasonal demand is equally important for a business operating in a competitive outdoor equipment market **[Ap]**

>   - A clear, justified conclusion based on evaluation of the issues

> - Accounting ratios provide objective, quantifiable data based on financial records → allows Erik to compare Norva's gross profit margin with previous years → identifies whether profitability is improving or declining → helps make informed decisions about pricing or cost reduction across the three stores
> - The current ratio shows whether Norva has sufficient current assets to cover its short-term liabilities → helps Erik assess whether the business can pay suppliers of outdoor clothing and equipment on time → reduces the risk of liquidity problems, particularly during quieter trading periods between seasons
> - Accounting ratios are based on historical data → do not reflect future market conditions → changes in demand for skiing or hiking equipment may not be captured → meaning ratios alone are insufficient for decisions about new product lines or store expansion
> - Accounting ratios do not capture customer satisfaction or competitor activity → qualitative factors are equally important for a seasonal outdoor retailer → market research and customer feedback would provide more useful information for decisions about product range or pricing strategy

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Luca is a small ice cream parlour in Brighton, England, opened in 2018 by Sofia Russo. It employs five part-time staff during the busy summer months. The business is highly seasonal, with the majority of its sales occurring between April and September. During winter, income falls significantly, but Luca still has fixed costs to meet, including rent and insurance. Sofia has limited experience of financial management and is considering expanding the business by adding a hot drinks menu to attract customers during the quieter months.

Evaluate the importance of cash flow forecasting for Luca.
parts.solutionMd:
A cash flow forecast is a financial document that predicts the expected cash inflows and outflows of a business over a future period **[K]**

Cash flow forecasting is particularly important for Luca because of the highly seasonal nature of its business **[K]**. A forecast allows Sofia to identify the winter months when cash inflows will fall sharply **[Ap]**, giving her time to arrange a bank overdraft or reduce spending before a cash shortage occurs** [An]**. Without this advance warning, Luca could run out of cash and be unable to pay its rent, insurance or suppliers during the quieter months** [An]**

However, Sofia has limited experience of financial management **[Ap]**, meaning any forecast she produces may be based on inaccurate estimates **[K]**. An unreliable forecast could give a misleading picture of Luca's finances, leading Sofia to make poor decisions about the timing of the hot drinks expansion **[An]**. Brighton's coastal weather is also unpredictable** [Ap]**, making it difficult to accurately forecast summer income, which reduces the overall reliability of the forecast** [An]**

Overall, cash flow forecasting is highly important for Luca given its seasonal trading pattern** [E]**, as the risk of winter cash shortages is significant for a small business with fixed costs to meet year-round **[Ap]**. While Sofia's limited financial experience is a challenge** [An]**, even an approximate forecast is better than none, as it provides a basis for planning and helps her avoid the most serious cash flow problems** [E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **12-mark 'evaluate' questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts linking points together to show clear cause and effect
>   - A clear, justified conclusion based on evaluation of the issues
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - A cash flow forecast helps Sofia plan the timing of the hot drinks expansion → ensuring she only invests when sufficient cash is available → reducing the risk of overextending the business financially
> - Seasonal businesses like Luca face predictable periods of low income → making a cash flow forecast particularly valuable for planning ahead → allowing Sofia to arrange finance before winter cash shortages occur
> - Inaccurate estimates in the forecast could lead Sofia to underestimate winter costs → resulting in a cash shortage that the forecast failed to predict → reducing the decision-making value of the document
> - A cash flow forecast could help Luca secure a bank overdraft for the winter months → by demonstrating to lenders that Sofia understands the business's finances → making it easier to access the support needed to survive quieter periods

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Folio is an independent bookshop in Edinburgh, Scotland, founded in 2010. It employs 12 staff across two stores and is well regarded for its carefully curated range of titles. Folio hosts regular author events that attract a loyal customer base and has grown steadily over 15 years of trading. The business is profitable but has recently experienced cash flow difficulties due to the high upfront cost of purchasing new stock and delays in receiving payment from schools and libraries that buy books in bulk. Folio's owner is concerned that these cash flow problems could affect the business's ability to operate effectively.

Evaluate the view that Folio should prioritise improving its cash flow over increasing its profit.
parts.solutionMd:
Cash flow refers to the movement of money into and out of a business, while profit is the amount remaining after all costs have been deducted from revenue **[K]**

Improving cash flow should be a priority for Folio because even a profitable business can fail if it runs out of cash** [K]**. Delays in receiving payment from schools and libraries** [Ap]** mean Folio may struggle to pay its 12 members of staff and purchase new stock on time, threatening its ability to operate its two stores effectively regardless of its underlying profitability **[An]**

However, long-term survival also depends on Folio maintaining and growing its profit** [K]**. If the business focuses solely on cash flow by reducing stock purchases or cutting costs** [An]**, it risks losing the carefully curated range that attracts its loyal customer base** [Ap]**, ultimately reducing sales and profit to a point where the business is no longer financially viable** [E]**

Overall, since Folio is already profitable** [Ap]**, addressing its immediate cash flow difficulties is the more urgent priority** [E]**. A business that cannot pay its staff or suppliers will face serious short-term consequences regardless of its profit levels **[K] [An]**. Once cash flow is stabilised, Folio can return its focus to growing profit through its author events and expanding its customer base **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **12-mark 'evaluate' questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts linking points together to show clear cause and effect
>   - A clear, justified conclusion based on evaluation of the issues
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Folio's delays in receiving payment from schools and libraries create a gap between revenue earned and cash received  → meaning the business may be unable to pay for new stock → leaving shelves understocked and disappointing the loyal customers who value Folio's curated range
> - Improving cash flow by chasing overdue payments from schools and libraries → would bring cash into the business more quickly → allowing Folio to restock and pay its 12 staff without disrupting day-to-day operations
> - Cutting costs to improve cash flow could reduce the quality and range of books stocked → undermining the reputation Folio has built over 15 years of trading → potentially causing loyal customers to shop elsewhere and reducing long-term profitability
> - A profitable business with poor cash flow can still become insolvent → making cash flow management the more pressing concern in the short term → while profitability can be grown again once the business's finances are stabilised

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Stamp is a small commercial printing business in Melbourne, Australia, founded in 2016 by Priya Sharma. It produces brochures, leaflets and business cards for local businesses and employs six full-time staff. Stamp is profitable but regularly experiences cash flow difficulties because many of its customers take up to 60 days to pay their invoices, while Stamp must pay its paper and ink suppliers within 30 days. Priya is concerned that this gap between money going out and money coming in could leave the business unable to meet its expenses.

Stamp is considering two options to improve its cash flow:

- Option 1: offer customers a discount for paying their invoices within 14 days
- Option 2: negotiate extended payment terms with its suppliers

Justify which one of these two options Stamp should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
Offering a discount for early payment incentivises customers to pay invoices sooner in exchange for a small reduction in the amount owed, while negotiating extended payment terms involves agreeing with suppliers to delay outgoing payments over a longer period** [K]**

One benefit of offering a discount is that it would encourage Stamp's customers to pay their invoices within 14 days rather than 60 ** [K] [Ap]**, bringing cash into the business much sooner and reducing the gap between cash inflows and outflows** [An]**

However, offering a discount reduces the amount Stamp receives for each job **[K]**, directly cutting its revenue and profit margins at a time when the business needs to remain financially stable **[Ap] [An]**

One benefit of negotiating extended payment terms with suppliers is that it delays cash leaving the business **[K]**, giving Stamp more time to collect payments from customers before it needs to pay for paper and ink** [Ap] [An]**

However, suppliers may be unwilling to agree to extended terms** [K]**, and if they refuse, Stamp would need to find an alternative solution to its cash flow problem, leaving Priya in a difficult position** [Ap] [An]**

Stamp should choose to negotiate extended payment terms with its suppliers **[E]**. Unlike offering discounts, extending supplier payment terms does not reduce Stamp's revenue **[K]**, meaning the business retains its full profit margin on every job **[An]**. By aligning its outgoing payments more closely with the 60-day period its customers take to pay **[Ap]**, Stamp can close the cash flow gap without sacrificing income, making this the more financially sustainable solution** [E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Offering a discount encourages Stamp's customers to pay quickly → bringing cash into the business sooner → reducing the risk of being unable to pay staff wages or supplier invoices on time
> - Extending supplier payment terms keeps cash in the business for longer → giving Stamp more flexibility to manage the gap between inflows and outflows → without reducing the revenue earned from each printing job
> - A discount reduces the amount received for each brochure, leaflet or business card produced → cutting profit margins for a small six-person business → making it harder for Stamp to cover its running costs and invest in future growth
> - If suppliers agree to extended payment terms → Stamp can better align its outgoing payments with its incoming customer receipts → resolving the cash flow problem without affecting customer relationships or revenue

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Golde is a small artisan bakery in Dublin, Ireland. It was founded ten years ago by Maeve O'Brien, who trained as a professional pastry chef. The bakery sells handmade sourdough bread, pastries and celebration cakes from a single shop in a busy market street. Maeve employs two part-time assistants who help with baking and serving customers.
> 
> Golde has built a strong reputation for quality and has a loyal local customer base, with many customers visiting several times a week. However, the cost of organic flour, butter and other specialist ingredients has risen sharply over the past year. As a result, the bakery is struggling to break even. Several other independent bakeries operate nearby, and a large supermarket recently opened on the same street.

Maeve is considering two options to lower Golde's break-even point.

- Option 1: Reduce variable costs by sourcing cheaper ingredients
- Option 2: Increase the selling prices of Golde's products

Justify which one of these two options Maeve should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
Break-even is the level of output at which total revenue equals total costs, meaning the business makes neither a profit nor a loss. Lowering the break-even point means Golde would need to sell fewer items before making a profit **[K]**

Reducing variable costs such as ingredient costs would lower the total cost per unit **[K]**, meaning that for each loaf or pastry Golde sells **[Ap]**, the contribution towards fixed costs increases, which would lower the break-even point** [An]**

However, cheaper ingredients could reduce the quality of Golde's handmade products **[K]**, damaging its reputation as an artisan bakery in Dublin **[Ap]**, and potentially causing loyal customers to stop buying from the shop **[An]**

Increasing selling prices would raise the revenue earned per unit **[K]**, meaning Golde earns more from each item it sells **[Ap]**, so each sale makes a greater contribution to fixed costs, lowering the break-even point **[An]**

However, raising prices could reduce demand **[K]**, particularly if customers in Dublin can buy similar baked goods from nearby competitors at lower prices **[Ap]**, meaning lower sales volume could offset the benefit of the higher price **[An]**

Maeve should choose Option 2 and increase selling prices** [E]**. Golde's loyal customer base suggests they value its handmade quality and are likely to accept a modest price rise **[Ap]**, making this a more reliable way to lower the break-even point than risking product quality by switching to cheaper ingredients **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer:**
> 
> - Cheaper ingredients reduce Golde's variable cost per unit → contribution per item increases → Golde needs to sell fewer items to break even → directly lowers the break-even point
> - Cheaper ingredients reduce quality of Golde's handmade products → loyal customers may switch to other artisan bakeries in Dublin → revenue falls → Golde may still struggle to break even despite lower costs
> - Increasing selling price raises revenue per unit → each item sold contributes more to Golde's fixed costs → fewer items need to be sold to cover total costs → break-even point falls
> - Higher prices could reduce customer demand → if sales volume falls significantly, total revenue may not increase → the higher price alone may not be enough to lower the break-even point

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Veld is a small flower farm on the outskirts of Amsterdam in the Netherlands. Petra van Dijk set up the business five years ago after leaving a career in horticulture. The farm grows tulips and sunflowers, which are hand-picked and sold in bunches to twelve local florists. Petra employs three full-time workers during the growing season.
> 
> Last year, Veld moved to a larger site to increase its capacity, resulting in significantly higher monthly rent. Despite selling a similar number of bunches as the previous year, the business is no longer making a profit. Petra prides herself on the high quality and presentation of Veld's flowers, which are wrapped in premium branded packaging. Several larger, commercial flower farms in the region supply the same florists and compete on price.

Petra is considering two options to help Veld return to profit.

- Option 1: Reduce fixed costs by moving back to a smaller site with lower rent
- Option 2: Reduce variable costs by using cheaper packaging for the flower bunches

Justify which one of these two options Petra should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
Fixed costs are costs that do not change with the level of output, such as rent, while variable costs change in proportion to output, such as packaging. Reducing either type of cost lowers the break-even point and can increase profit **[K]**

Moving to a smaller site would directly reduce Veld's fixed costs** [K]**, meaning total costs fall at every level of output. Since higher rent has been identified as the cause of Veld's profitability problem **[Ap]**, this would have an immediate impact on the break-even point** [An]**

However, a smaller site could reduce the number of tulips and sunflowers Veld is able to grow** [K]**, limiting the bunches available for local florists in Amsterdam **[Ap]**, and reducing revenue if orders cannot be fulfilled **[An]**

Using cheaper packaging would reduce Veld's variable costs per bunch **[K]**, meaning the contribution from each bunch sold to florists increases** [Ap]**, which also lowers the break-even point** [An]**

However, cheaper packaging could reduce the visual appeal of Veld's flower bunches** [K]**, making them less attractive to the florists who buy from the farm **[Ap]**, potentially causing them to switch to alternative suppliers and reducing Veld's revenue** [An]**

Petra should choose Option 1 and move to a smaller site** [E]**. Since the rise in rent has been directly identified as the cause of the profit problem **[Ap]**, reducing this fixed cost would have a much greater impact on profitability than the relatively small savings achievable through cheaper packaging** [E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer:**
> 
> - Moving to a smaller site reduces Veld's rent → fixed costs fall → total costs fall at every level of output → Veld reaches break-even at a lower level of output → directly addresses the cause of the profit problem
> - A smaller site limits growing space → fewer tulips and sunflowers can be produced → Veld cannot fulfil all florist orders → revenue may fall → reduced income could cancel out the savings from lower rent
> - Cheaper packaging reduces Veld's variable cost per bunch → contribution per unit increases → fewer bunches need to be sold to cover fixed costs → break-even point falls
> - Lower quality packaging reduces the visual appeal of flower bunches → local florists may choose suppliers with better presentation → Veld loses customers → revenue falls → savings on packaging are outweighed by lost sales

> **[case-study]**
> Lumea is a small candle-making business based in Lisbon, Portugal. Sofia Antunes founded the business three years ago after leaving a career as a chemist. Lumea produces a range of scented soy candles by hand, each made using premium soy wax, essential oils and recycled glass jars. The candles are sold through a small shop in a popular tourist area of central Lisbon and through the business website, which attracts customers across Europe. Sofia employs one full-time assistant.

As a result, Lumea is currently selling below its break-even point and is making a loss.

Evaluate the view that Lumea should reduce its variable costs in order to return to profit.
parts.solutionMd:
Variable costs are costs that change directly with the level of output** [K]**, such as the soy wax and essential oils used in Lumea's candles **[Ap]**. Reducing variable costs lowers the cost per unit, which increases contribution per candle and lowers the break-even point** [An]**

Reducing variable costs would directly address the 20% rise in material costs that has caused Lumea to fall below its break-even point **[Ap]**. If Sofia sourced cheaper soy wax or essential oils** [K]**, the cost per candle would fall, meaning Lumea would need to sell fewer candles to cover its fixed costs and return to profit **[An]**

However, Lumea's reputation is built on using premium natural ingredients to produce high-quality scented candles **[Ap]**, and cheaper materials could reduce the quality and scent performance of the product **[K]**, risking the loyalty of regular customers and European online buyers who pay a premium specifically for this quality** [An]**. A better option may be to increase the selling price, which would raise contribution per unit without compromising product quality** [E]**

Overall, reducing variable costs is not the most effective long-term solution for Lumea** [E]**. Although it would lower the break-even point, the risk of damaging product quality and reputation in a competitive tourist area **[Ap]** outweighs the benefit. Increasing the selling price would be a safer approach **[E]**, as Lumea's premium positioning and loyal customer base **[Ap]** suggest customers are likely to accept a modest price rise without switching to alternatives** [Ap]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **12-mark 'evaluate' questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts linking points together to show clear cause and effect
>   - A clear, justified conclusion based on evaluation of the issues
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer:**
> 
> - Soy wax and essential oil costs have risen by 20% → variable cost per candle increases → Lumea falls below its break-even point → sourcing cheaper materials would lower variable cost per unit → contribution per candle increases → fewer candles need to be sold to break even
> - Cheaper ingredients reduce candle quality and scent performance → regular customers and European online buyers notice the difference → sales volume falls → revenue decreases → Lumea may still struggle to reach break-even despite lower costs
> - Increasing the selling price would raise revenue per candle → contribution per unit increases → break-even point falls → Lumea returns to profit without risking the product quality that underpins its reputation
> - Lumea's premium positioning and tourist-area location suggest price-inelastic demand → customers visit specifically for high-quality sustainable candles → a modest price increase is unlikely to significantly reduce sales volume → making a price rise a lower-risk route back to profitability than cutting ingredient quality

> Kemble is a social enterprise based in Copenhagen, Denmark, that produces handcrafted furniture from reclaimed wood. Profit is the surplus remaining after total costs have been deducted from revenue** [K]**. For a social enterprise like Kemble, generating profit must be balanced against fulfilling its social objectives** [K]**

Profit is essential for Kemble's long-term survival** [K]**, as without sufficient income to cover its rising timber costs and operating expenses the business would be unable to continue** [Ap]**, meaning the social mission of employing people with disabilities and those facing long-term unemployment could not be sustained** [An]**

However, as a social enterprise, Kemble exists specifically to create social value rather than maximise profit** [K]**. The business was founded to provide meaningful employment for disadvantaged people in Bristol** [Ap]**, meaning success is more appropriately measured by the number of people supported and the impact on their lives, rather than the level of profit generated **[An]**

Overall, profit is important for Kemble but is not its most important objective **[E]**. Without generating sufficient income the business could not survive **[K]**, but since Kemble was founded specifically to provide employment for people who struggle to find work **[Ap**], its social impact is a more meaningful measure of success than profit alone **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **12-mark 'evaluate' questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts linking points together to show clear cause and effect
>   - A clear, justified conclusion based on evaluation of the issues
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer:**

> - Kemble was founded specifically to provide employment for disadvantaged people in Bristol → social impact is the primary measure of success for a social enterprise → profit is a means to an end rather than the main objective → making profit the most important objective would misrepresent the purpose of the business
