However, the income statement only reflects past financial performance and may not indicate future trading potential **[K]**. The underperforming shop has only been open for two years and may still be building its customer base in a new residential area of Riga **[Ap]**, meaning a decision based solely on historical profit figures could lead to premature closure **[An]**. A statement of financial position would also be valuable **[E]**, as it reveals the assets held by the shop, helping the family assess the full financial impact of closure **[An]**

Overall, the statement of comprehensive income is a useful starting point for the Bērziņš family **[E]**, as it clearly shows which shop is underperforming **[Ap]**. However, it should not be the only document consulted, since profit figures alone do not reveal liquidity or asset values, and a decision based purely on historical data could overlook the shop's longer-term potential **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

>

> - The income statement only shows historical data → does not reflect the future trading potential of the new Riga location → the shop may become profitable once it builds a loyal customer base in the residential area → closing based on two years of data alone could be a costly mistake
> - A statement of financial position would also be useful → reveals assets held by the underperforming shop such as ovens and equipment → helps the family understand the financial consequences of closure → providing a more complete picture than the income statement alone

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Trevi is a small artisan pasta-making business in Rome, Italy, founded eight years ago by Marco Esposito. The business produces fresh pasta and sauces which are sold to local restaurants and from a small shop near the city centre. Trevi employs five members of staff.
> 
> Marco took out a bank loan four years ago to purchase pasta-making equipment, and a portion of this loan remains outstanding. Trevi's most recent statement of comprehensive income shows that the business has generated a healthy level of profit this year for the first time since the loan was taken out. Marco must now decide how to use this profit.

Marco is considering two options for using Trevi's profit.

- Option 1: Reinvest the profit into new, more efficient pasta-making machinery
- Option 2: Use the profit to repay part of the outstanding bank loan

Justify which one of these two options Marco should choose
parts.solutionMd:
Profit is the surplus remaining after all costs have been deducted from revenue **[K]**, as shown in the statement of comprehensive income. It can be reinvested into the business or used to reduce liabilities shown on the statement of financial position **[K]**

Investing in new machinery would increase Trevi's production capacity **[K]**, allowing Marco to produce larger quantities of fresh pasta to supply more restaurants in Rome **[Ap]**, potentially increasing revenue and generating even greater profit in future years **[An]**

However, purchasing new machinery would reduce Trevi's cash reserves **[K]**, meaning the business may have less financial flexibility if unexpected costs arise **[Ap]**, and would not reduce the ongoing interest payments on the existing bank loan **[An]**

Using profit to repay part of the loan would reduce Trevi's non-current liabilities **[K]**, lowering the annual interest payments the business must make **[Ap]**, which would reduce expenses and increase future operating profit shown in the income statement **[An]**

However, repaying the loan would not directly increase Trevi's production capacity or revenue **[K]**], meaning the business could miss the opportunity to grow by investing in more efficient equipment **[Ap]**, limiting the long-term profitability of the pasta business **[An]**

Marco should choose Option 1 and reinvest in new machinery **[E]**. As Trevi has built a strong reputation supplying local restaurants over eight years **[Ap]**, investing in greater production capacity is more likely to generate sustainable profit growth than reducing loan repayments, particularly if interest costs on the loan are manageable** [E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer:**
> 
> - New machinery increases production capacity → Trevi can supply more restaurants in Rome → revenue increases → profit  grows further → generating a greater long-term return than the cost of the machinery
> - Purchasing new machinery reduces cash reserves → less financial flexibility if costs rise unexpectedly → Trevi may struggle to meet short-term obligations → making loan repayment the safer short-term option
> - Repaying part of the bank loan reduces non-current liabilities → annual interest payments fall → operating expenses decrease → operating profit shown in the income statement improves without needing to increase revenue
> - Repaying the loan does not increase production capacity → Trevi's revenue remains unchanged → the business cannot grow its customer base or supply more restaurants → limiting future profit growth compared with investing in new machinery

parts.problemMd: Explain **one **reason why some businesses use crowdfunding as a source of finance.
parts.solutionMd:

> - Crowdfunding raises awareness of a business and its products at the same time as generating finance **[1 mark]**, as the campaign itself acts as a form of marketing that reaches a wide audience through online platforms **[1 mark]**, meaning the business benefits from both the funds raised and increased public interest in its product before it has even launched **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd: Explain **one **disadvantage to a business of using retained profits to purchase goods and services.
parts.solutionMd:
Using retained profits means the money is no longer available for other purposes within the business **[1 mark]**, such as paying dividends to shareholders or funding other investments that could help the business to grow **[1 mark]**, which may create tension with shareholders who expect a financial return and could make the business less attractive to potential investors **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award 1 mark for a disadvantage to a business of using retained profit to purchase goods and services, plus 2 further marks for explaining this reason, for a maximum of 3 marks.
> 
> - A business must have generated sufficient profits before it can use retained profits as a source of finance **[1 mark]**, meaning this option is not available to new businesses or those that have recently made a loss **[1 mark]**, leaving them with no choice but to seek more expensive external sources of finance such as bank loans **[1 mark]**
> - Accumulating enough retained profit to fund a significant purchase can take a long time **[1 mark]**, meaning the business may have to delay important investments in new equipment, stock or technology while it builds up sufficient funds **[1 mark]**, potentially putting it at a competitive disadvantage compared to rivals who are able to finance their purchases more quickly **[1 mark]**
> - Accept any other appropriate response.

> 
> No marks are awarded for a definition alone.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> *Posh Pets Spain (PPS)* is a pet hotel in the village of Alhaurin el Grande, Spain. It is run by Rachel Goutorbe, an animal enthusiast, and her team of four pet specialists. *PPS *offers overnight accommodation with room for seven dogs or cats, a pet grooming service and a shop selling pet products, such as dog coats and dog leads. Pet grooming involves washing, cutting and combing a pet’s coat.

*PPS *is looking to build another eight kennels with Closed-circuit television (CCTV) in its pet hotel. To do this it will need €7 500.

*PPS *is considering two options:

- **Option 1:** using Rachel’s personal savings
- **Option 2:** taking out a small bank loan.

Justify which **one **of these two options *PPS *should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
Personal savings are funds from the owner's own money used to finance the business, while a bank loan is a fixed sum borrowed from a bank and repaid with interest over an agreed period **[K]**

One benefit of using Rachel's personal savings is that PPS would not need to make any interest repayments **[K]**, keeping costs low for a small pet hotel with only four staff and limited capacity for seven dogs or cats** [Ap] [An]**

However, Rachel may not have sufficient personal savings to cover the full €7,500 needed to build the eight new kennels and install CCTV** [Ap] [K]**, and using all of her savings would leave her with no financial safety net if unexpected costs arose** [An]**

One benefit of a bank loan is that it would provide PPS with the full €7,500 immediately **[K]**, allowing building work on the new kennels and CCTV installation to begin without delay** [Ap] [An]**

However, a bank loan requires PPS to make regular interest repayments** [K]**, which would increase the business's costs and could place financial pressure on a small pet hotel whose income depends on the number of animals booked in at any one time** [Ap] [An]**

PPS should choose Option 1: Rachel's personal savings **[E]**. As a small business run by one owner with a team of four specialists** [Ap]**, taking on debt through a bank loan could create significant financial pressure if bookings are low** [An]**. Using personal savings eliminates interest costs entirely, keeping PPS financially stable while it expands its kennels and grows its capacity **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Personal savings give Rachel immediate access to funds without the need for a bank application or approval process → allowing building work on the new kennels to begin quickly → helping PPS to increase its capacity and take on more bookings sooner
> - A bank loan provides the certainty of receiving the full €7,500 even if Rachel's personal savings fall short → ensuring the project can be completed in full → allowing PPS to offer all eight new kennels with CCTV to customers
> - Interest repayments on a bank loan would reduce PPS's profit margins → making it harder for the small business to cover its running costs → suggesting personal savings are the more financially prudent option
> - Building eight new kennels would increase PPS's capacity significantly → generating additional revenue from more overnight bookings and grooming appointments → which over time could comfortably cover the cost of bank loan repayments

> *Saha *is a small business in Türkiye (formerly known as Turkey) that opened in 2020 with 15 employees. It designs and manufactures robots which are used in hospitals, hotels and restaurants. In hospitals its robots are used to move medical supplies between departments. In hotels and restaurants, the robots are used to welcome customers as they arrive and deliver food and drinks to hotel rooms and restaurant tables. *Saha *provides a seven day a week customer service for all businesses buying its robots.

When *Saha *expands its business it will require additional finance. It is considering two options:

- **Option 2:** loan capital.

Justify which **one **of these two options *Saha *should choose.

> 
> *AWG’s* increasing product range now includes jumpers, dresses, shirts and baby clothes. These are produced in small workshops that employ family and friends. Waste is kept to a minimum and any leftover material is used to make scarves and hats. The business has one store in Iceland. It uses its website to advertise and sell its clothing online to customers in other countries. The business has received the Icelandic Design Award for its contribution to the environment.

parts.solutionMd:
Venture capital is finance provided by investors in exchange for a share of ownership and a role in business decisions, while franchising involves allowing individuals to operate a business using an established brand and model in exchange for a fee** [K]**

However, venture capitalists take a share of ownership and decision-making in AWG **[K]**, which could put pressure on the business to prioritise profit over its social objective of using natural materials and reducing waste **[Ap]**, potentially compromising the values that earned it the Icelandic Design Award** [An]**

One benefit of franchising is that franchisees fund the opening of new stores themselves **[K]**, allowing AWG to expand across Iceland without needing to raise external finance or give up ownership of the business **[Ap] [An]**

However, AWG may struggle to ensure that franchisees maintain its strict commitment to environmentally friendly materials and production methods **[Ap] [K]**, risking damage to the brand and its award-winning reputation if standards are not upheld** [An]**

AWG should choose franchising **[E]**. As a business whose identity is built around its social and environmental values **[Ap]**, inviting venture capitalists into the business risks those values being overridden by investors focused on financial returns** [An]**. parts.problemMd: Explain **one **way a business could use market research information.
parts.solutionMd:
A business could use market research information to identify what customers need and want from a product **[1 mark]**, allowing it to adapt existing products or develop new ones that better match customer preferences **[1 mark]**, making it more likely that the product will sell successfully and generate profit for the business **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> **Alternative ways to answer:**
> 
> - A business could use market research data to set prices at a level customers are willing to pay  **[1 mark]**, ensuring it does not charge so much that customers switch to a competitor's product instead  **[1 mark]**, helping the business maintain its market share and achieve its sales targets  **[1 mark]**
> - A business could use market research information to identify gaps in the market where customer needs are not currently being met  **[1 mark]**, allowing it to develop and launch new products to fill those gaps before its competitors do  **[1 mark]**, giving the business a competitive advantage and the opportunity to attract new customers  **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Most people recognise Heinz for the phrase ‘57 varieties’ even though it now produces many more than the original 57 varieties. H J Heinz, the founder of the Heinz business, believed the phrase sounded lucky.
> 
> *Kraft Heinz* is a world-wide producer of food products. It was formed from the merger of Kraft Foods and Heinz in 2015. This created the third largest food and drinks business in the USA and the fifth largest food and drinks business in the world.
> 
> *Kraft Heinz* has over 24 different brands, including Greenseas in Australia and Nutri+Plus in New Zealand. America has the largest number of brands from Maxwell House to Cool Whip. *Kraft Heinz* produces many different products including tomato sauce, ‘Mac&Cheese’, pasta and its famous baked beans that are used and eaten by many people.
> 
> *Kraft Heinz* uses many methods to advertise its products. These include posters, billboards and leaflets in supermarkets.

*Kraft Heinz* is introducing a new variety of tomato sauce and has made changes to the recipe for its Mac&Cheese.

Analyse the benefits to *Kraft Heinz* of using social media to collect market research data.
parts.solutionMd:
Social media allows Kraft Heinz to gather market research data from a very large number of customers across the world at low cost** [1 mark]**, which is particularly valuable for a business with over 24 brands operating in multiple countries, as it can reach existing customers of brands such as Greenseas and Maxwell House without the expense of running focus groups or surveys **[1 mark]**, meaning Kraft Heinz can collect data quickly and affordably to inform decisions about new products such as its new variety of tomato sauce **[1 mark]**

Social media platforms allow customers to post comments, reviews and reactions about Kraft Heinz products **[1 mark]**, providing qualitative data that gives the business a deeper understanding of how customers feel about changes such as the new Mac&Cheese recipe **[1 mark]**, allowing Kraft Heinz to identify any negative reactions early and make further adjustments before rolling the product out on a larger scale, reducing the risk of a costly failure **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award up to 2 marks for identifying benefits to Kraft Heinz of using social media to collect market research data.
> 
> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for applying those benefits to Kraft Heinz's specific context.
> 
> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for explaining the consequences of those benefits for Kraft Heinz.
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer:**
> 
> - Social media provides Kraft Heinz with real-time feedback from customers as soon as a new product or recipe change is announced **[1 mark]**, allowing the business to monitor reactions to the new tomato sauce variety as they happen rather than waiting weeks for the results of traditional research methods **[1 mark]**, enabling Kraft Heinz to respond quickly to any concerns and make adjustments before committing to full-scale production **[1 mark]**
> - Kraft Heinz can use social media to target specific groups of customers when collecting market research data **[1 mark]**, for example gathering feedback from health-conscious consumers about its Nutri+Plus brand or from families about Mac&Cheese **[1 mark]**, ensuring the data collected is relevant to each product and more useful for making decisions about product development **[1 mark]**
> 
> Answers that list six benefits of using social media to collect market research data with no explanation will get a maximum of 1 mark.
> 
> No marks are awarded for a definition alone.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one **disadvantage of using questionnaires as a method of market research.
parts.solutionMd:
Questionnaires often have a low response rate, meaning many people choose not to complete or return them **[1 mark]**, which reduces the size of the sample and may mean the results do not accurately represent the views of all customers **[1 mark]**, leading the business to make decisions based on unreliable data that could result in developing products that do not meet the needs of its target market **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award 1 mark for identifying a valid disadvantage of using questionnaires. 2 further marks are awarded for explaining the disadvantage, for a maximum of 3 marks.
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer:**
> 
> - Questionnaires use fixed questions, which means the business cannot ask follow-up questions if a respondent gives an interesting or unexpected answer **[1 mark]**, limiting the depth of information gathered compared to methods such as focus groups **[1 mark]**, meaning the business may miss important insights about customer opinions that could have been uncovered through further questioning **[1 mark]**
> - Respondents may misunderstand or misinterpret the questions in a questionnaire **[1 mark]**, particularly if the questions are poorly worded or use language that customers are not familiar with **[1 mark]**, producing inaccurate responses that lead to unreliable data and could cause the business to make poor decisions about its products or marketing **[1 mark]**
> - Accept any other appropriate response.
> 
> Answers that list three disadvantages of questionnaires with no explanation will get a maximum of 1 mark.
> 
> No marks are awarded for a definition alone.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one **benefit to a business of using secondary market research.
parts.solutionMd:
Secondary research is cheaper than primary research because the data has already been collected and published by others **[1 mark]**, meaning a business can access market reports, government statistics or internet sources without the cost of designing and conducting its own surveys or focus groups **[1 mark]**, allowing businesses with limited budgets to gather useful market information and make informed decisions without spending large amounts of money **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award 1 mark for identifying a valid benefit of using secondary market research. 2 further marks are awarded for explaining the benefit, for a maximum of 3 marks.
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer:**
> 
> - Secondary research saves time because the data already exists and can be accessed quickly **[1 mark]**, allowing a business to gather information about the market, competitors or customer trends without waiting weeks for primary research to be completed **[1 mark]**, meaning the business can make faster decisions about product development or marketing strategies **[1 mark]**
> - Secondary research, such as government reports or market research reports, is often based on very large samples of data **[1 mark]**, giving the business a broad overview of market trends that would be too expensive and time-consuming to collect through primary research alone **[1 mark]**, providing a reliable foundation on which to base decisions before investing in more specific primary research **[1 mark]**
> - Accept any other appropriate response.
> 
> Answers that list three benefits of secondary market research with no explanation will get a maximum of 1 mark.
> 
> No marks are awarded for a definition alone.

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** reason why a business would use primary research.
parts.solutionMd:
A business would use primary research when it needs data that is specific to its own products, customers or market **[1 mark]**, as secondary research may be too general or not directly relevant to the exact question the business is trying to answer **[1 mark]**, allowing the business to gather information tailored precisely to its needs, such as customer opinions on a new product it is planning to launch **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award 1 mark for a reason why primary research would be used by a business, plus 2 further marks for explaining why it would be used by a business, for a maximum of 3 marks.
> 
> - A business would use primary research when it needs the most up-to-date information about its customers or market **[1 mark]**, as secondary research may have been collected months or years ago and may no longer accurately reflect the market **[1 mark]**, ensuring the business makes decisions based on current data rather than outdated information that could lead to poor choices **[1 mark]**
> - A business would use primary research because the data it collects is not available to its competitors **[1 mark]**, as the information is gathered specifically for that business and is not published or shared publicly **[1 mark]**, giving the business a competitive advantage by allowing it to act on exclusive insights about customer needs before rivals are aware of the same trends **[1 mark]**
> - Accept any other appropriate response.
> 
> Answers that list three reasons why a business would use primary research with no explanation will get a maximum of 1 mark.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> *TUI *is a holiday business that has over 100 years of experience. It offers customers a variety of holidays including staying in hotels, and river and ocean-going cruises. There are many extras that it offers to holiday makers including: car hire, extensions to the holiday and arranging day trips at all its holiday destinations.
> 
> The business is well known and flies its customers to over 180 destinations around the world, including Greece, Turkey and Spain. It has 1,600 travel agencies and 27 million customers. Holidays can be booked by visiting a travel agency or online.
> 
> *TUI *has holidays to meet the needs of all its customers: families, children, couples and those with disabilities.

*TUI *constantly checks for customer feedback and comments on its holidays, including hotel stays and cruises. It is considering the following two options to gain the most up-to-date views:

- **Option 1**: using the internet** **
- **Option 2**: asking customers to complete a questionnaire.

Justify which **one **of these two options *TUI *should use.
parts.solutionMd:
Market research is the process of collecting information about customers' views and needs to help a business make decisions. Primary research collects new data directly from customers, while using the internet allows TUI to access existing customer feedback from online reviews and social media **[K]**

Using the internet allows TUI to access customer reviews and comments posted on social media and review websites **[K]** across its 180 destinations **[Ap]**, enabling the business to gather large amounts of real-time feedback from its 27 million customers without spending money on designing and distributing questionnaires **[An]**

However, online reviews may be unreliable **[K]** as they tend to be written by customers who had an extremely positive or negative experience rather than the majority of TUI's holidaymakers **[Ap]**, meaning the data may not accurately represent most customers' views and could lead TUI to make poor decisions about its holidays **[An]**

A questionnaire allows TUI to design specific questions about the exact aspects of its service it wants feedback on **[K]**, such as the quality of hotel stays and cruises **[Ap]**, ensuring the data gathered is directly relevant and more useful for decision-making **[An]**

However, questionnaires may suffer from a low response rate **[K]** as many of TUI's 27 million customers may not take the time to complete them **[Ap]**, reducing the size of the sample and making the results less representative of all holidaymakers **[An]**

TUI should use questionnaires **[E]** as they allow the business to gather specific, targeted feedback on hotel stays and cruises **[Ap] **rather than relying on general online comments that TUI cannot control. The internet would be less suitable, as the data collected may be unrepresentative and unreliable, making it a weaker basis for decision-making **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer:**
> 
> - Using the internet gives TUI access to customer reviews and social media comments posted across its 180 destinations → with 27 million customers there is a large volume of existing feedback available → allowing TUI to monitor customer views in real time without the cost of producing and distributing questionnaires
> - Online reviews may be written only by customers with strong opinions → meaning the data may not represent the views of the majority of TUI's holidaymakers → which could lead TUI to make inaccurate decisions about which aspects of its holidays to improve
> - A questionnaire allows TUI to ask specific questions about hotel stays and cruises → generating data that is directly relevant to the feedback TUI wants → so Rachel and the management team can make well-informed decisions about which holiday products to improve
> - Questionnaires may have a low response rate → meaning TUI receives replies from only a small proportion of its 27 million customers → making the results less reliable and harder to use as the basis for major business decisions TUI should use the internet as it can reach a far larger number of customers quickly

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> *The Better Toy Store (TBTS)* is a children’s toy shop. *TBTS *has three shops in Singapore. Two of the shops are located in busy shopping malls, and the third is located at the Jewel Changi Airport. *TBTS *has a website for customers looking to buy toys online.
> 
> *TBTS *selects toys to sell that are excellent for play, value, design and quality. All *TBTS *toys are environmentally friendly.

*TBTS *is planning to introduce a new range of toys for four-year-old children. It will need to carry out some research from its customers, including children and parents, to find out what they want.

*TBTS *is considering two options:

- **Option 1: **hand out questionnaires to customers that visit the shops
- **Option 2: **hold focus group meetings with parents and their children.

Justify which **one **of these two options *TBTS *should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
A questionnaire uses written questions given directly to customers, while a focus group brings a small group of people together to share opinions in depth **[K]**

Handing questionnaires to customers at TBTS's three shops allows the business to collect feedback from a large number of parents **[K]** across its shopping mall and Jewel Changi Airport locations **[Ap]**, gathering views on the new toy range quickly and at low cost **[An]**

However, questionnaires would be ineffective for gathering feedback from four-year-old children **[K]** as they are too young to read or write **[Ap]**, meaning TBTS would only receive the views of parents rather than the children who will actually use the toys **[An]**

A focus group allows TBTS to bring parents and children together to respond to new toy ideas **[K]**, with a moderator observing children's reactions and asking parents about features such as quality and environmental friendliness **[Ap]**, providing rich qualitative data that a questionnaire could not capture **[An]**

However, focus groups involve only a small number of participants **[K]**, so results may not represent all of TBTS's customers across its three stores **[Ap]**, and they can be more costly and time-consuming to organise **[An]**

TBTS should use focus groups **[E] **because four-year-old children cannot complete questionnaires, making it impossible to gather opinions from those who will use the toys **[Ap]**. Observing how children respond to toy ideas gives TBTS more relevant data for developing its new range than questionnaires could provide **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer:**
> 
> - Questionnaires can be completed anonymously → meaning parents may give more honest and candid feedback than they would face-to-face in a focus group → providing TBTS with more reliable data on what customers want from the new toy range
> - Questionnaires use fixed questions with no opportunity to probe interesting responses → if a parent mentions something useful about what their child enjoys, TBTS cannot follow up for more detail → resulting in shallow data that may miss important insights for developing the new toy range
> - Focus groups allow TBTS to show children physical toy prototypes or images of new designs → children can interact with them and give immediate, natural reactions → providing genuine insight into whether the new toys are engaging and enjoyable for four-year-olds
> - Parents may dominate focus group discussions → four-year-old children may be reluctant to speak freely in front of strangers or become easily distracted → meaning their genuine views may not be fully captured, reducing the usefulness of the research

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> *Nantgwynfaen Organic Farm (NOF)* is a farm growing a range of fruit and vegetables. It has a farm shop and offers accommodation with breakfast. It was set up by Amanda and Ken Edwards in West Wales, UK.
> 
> *NOF *supports farmers by selling local organic produce in its farm shop. The produce from the farm shop is served to the visitors staying overnight at the farm.
> 
> *NOF *is committed to being environmentally friendly by recycling, avoiding the use of packaging and reducing the use of electricity.

*NOF *is looking to increase the number of visitors to the farm. It will need to carry out some research as to what potential visitors will want.

To do this *NOF *is considering two options:

- **Option 1:** handing out questionnaires at local retailers
- **Option 2:** using the internet to research other farms.

Justify which **one **of these two options *NOF *should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
A questionnaire collects primary data directly from customers, while using the internet accesses existing secondary data about other businesses** [K]**

Handing questionnaires to people at local retailers allows NOF to gather first-hand data **[K] **from local people who could become visitors to the farm **[Ap]**, helping Amanda and Ken find out what potential customers want from a farm stay, such as accommodation preferences or activities** [An]**

However, questionnaires at local retailers only reach people who shop at those specific stores **[K]**, meaning the results may not represent all potential visitors, such as tourists from outside West Wales **[Ap] **who could also be attracted to NOF **[An]**

Researching other farm accommodation businesses online allows NOF to identify what features and services attract visitors **[K]** to similar organic farm stays **[Ap]**, giving Amanda and Ken a quick, cost-free overview of what works well for comparable businesses **[An]**

However, internet research about other farms cannot reveal what NOF's own potential visitors specifically want **[K]**, as the data relates to customers of different businesses rather than people considering a stay at the farm in West Wales **[Ap]**, making it less directly useful for NOF **[An]**

NOF should use questionnaires **[E] **as they gather first-hand data directly from local people who could become visitors, providing specific and relevant information that internet research about other farms **[Ap] **cannot offer **[An]**. Internet research shows what competitors offer rather than what NOF's own customers want, making it a weaker basis for decisions about increasing visitor numbers **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer:**
> 
> - Questionnaires can include specific questions about NOF's own offering → such as whether visitors would like to learn about organic farming or sample local produce from the farm shop → helping Amanda and Ken tailor the farm experience to attract more visitors
> - Many people approached at local retailers may be too busy to stop and complete a questionnaire → reducing the number of responses NOF receives → making it harder to draw reliable conclusions about what potential visitors want from a farm stay
> - Reading online customer reviews of other farm stays allows NOF to identify what visitors commonly enjoy or complain about → helping Amanda and Ken understand what to prioritise when developing their accommodation offering → without spending any money on primary research
> - Information found online about other farms may be outdated → meaning it does not accurately reflect what visitors currently want → leading NOF to make decisions based on data that no longer represents the preferences of today's customers
> - NOF should use the internet as it is a small farm with limited resources and staff → conducting questionnaires would take time away from running the farm shop and accommodation → whereas internet research provides a cost-free starting point for understanding what features attract visitors to similar farm stays

Emirates should use focus groups **[E] **as understanding the specific reasons why passenger ratings fell in 2017 requires in-depth qualitative data that questionnaires cannot provide **[An]**. parts.solutionMd:

parts.solutionMd:
**Method 1:**

$725 . 92 \times 2 = 1451 . 84$

$1451 . 84 \times 0 . 125 = 181 . 48$ **[1 mark]**

$1451 . 84 - 181 . 48 =$ **1270.36** **[1 mark]**

$635 . 18 \times 2 =$ **1270.36** **[1 mark]**

>

> **[exam-tip]**

Remember that you can calculate the discount either by finding 12.5% and subtracting it, or by multiplying by 0.875 (i.e. $1 - 0 . 125$) directly. Both approaches are equally valid. > *TUI *is a holiday business that has over 100 years of experience. It offers customers a variety of holidays including staying in hotels, and river and ocean-going cruises. There are many extras that it offers to holiday makers including: car hire, extensions to the holiday and arranging day trips at all its holiday destinations.
> 
> The business is well known and flies its customers to over 180 destinations around the world, including Greece, Turkey and Spain. It has 1,600 travel agencies and 27 million customers. Holidays can be booked by visiting a travel agency or online.
> 
> *TUI *has holidays to meet the needs of all its customers: families, children, couples and those with disabilities.

Analyse how *TUI *could make use of the Boston Matrix to review all the different types of holidays it offers.
parts.solutionMd:
TUI could use the Boston Matrix to identify which of its holidays are Stars, meaning they have high market share and strong demand** [1 mark]**. Holidays to popular destinations such as Greece and Spain are likely to be Stars as they attract large numbers of TUI's 27 million customers **[1 mark]**, so TUI should continue to invest in these to keep them competitive and protect its position as a leading holiday business **[1 mark]**

The Boston Matrix could also help TUI identify any Dogs in its range — holidays with low market share and little growth **[1 mark]**. If certain products such as river cruises are not selling well compared to TUI's other holidays **[1 mark]**, TUI could decide to remove them from its range and use the money saved to improve its more popular holidays, such as adding more day trips and extras at its destinations **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award up to 2 marks for identifying points about how TUI could use the Boston Matrix to review its holidays.
> 
> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for applying the points to TUI's context.
> 
> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for explaining how using the Boston Matrix helps TUI as a business.
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - TUI could use the Boston Matrix to identify any Question Marks in its product range **[1 mark]**. Ocean cruises may be a growing market but TUI may not yet have a large share of it compared to more established rivals **[1 mark]**, so TUI could decide to invest more in this area to try to turn it into a Star and attract a new type of customer **[1 mark]**
> - TUI could use the Boston Matrix to identify its Cash Cows — holidays that have a high market share but are in a market that is no longer growing **[1 mark]**. Established hotel holidays in Spain and Turkey may fall into this category **[1 mark]**, meaning TUI can rely on these to generate steady income while using the profits to invest in newer holiday products or improve its online booking platform **[1 mark]**
> 
> Answers that list six points about the Boston Matrix with no explanation will get a maximum of 1 mark.
> 
> No marks are awarded for a definition alone.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> The first *Premier Inn* hotel was opened in 1987. *Premier Inn *now has over 820 hotels in the UK, United Arab Emirates (UAE) and India with over 83,000 rooms. It has recently expanded by opening the first *Premier Inn *in Germany and has plans to open more in other countries.
> 
> The majority of the hotels have restaurants with facilities for guests to buy meals and drinks.

To encourage people to stay at a new German hotel, *Premier Inn* offers a 12.5% discount on a room for the first night only.

The price for one night is €89.25.

Calculate, to two decimal places, the price for the first night after the discount has been applied. You are advised to show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
$89 . 25 \times 0 . 125 = 11 . 16$ **[1 mark]**

$89 . 25 - 11 . 16 = \text{EUR}  78 . 09$ **[1 mark]**

**Final answer:** **EUR 78.09**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award 1 mark for correctly calculating the discount: $89 . 25 \times 0 . 125 = 11 . 16$
> 
> Award 1 mark for subtracting the discount to reach the final answer of $78 . 09$
> 
> Award full marks for a correct final answer without working shown
> 
> If the final answer is incorrect, award 1 mark for correct workings (e.g. correctly calculating the discount amount)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always show your working in calculation questions — even if you arrive at the correct answer, showing your method ensures you can still pick up marks if you make a small arithmetic error at the end. A common approach here is to multiply the price by 0.125 to find the discount, then subtract it from the original price. Alternatively, you could multiply by 0.875 (i.e. $1 - 0 . 125$) to go straight to the discounted price. Make sure you round your final answer to two decimal places as instructed.

**[2 marks]**

> - Test marketing helps a business to predict how much demand there will be for a new product **[1 mark]**, as sales figures from the test area can be used to estimate how many units will sell nationally **[1 mark]**, meaning the business can plan its production levels more accurately and avoid producing too much or too little stock **[1 mark]**

> **[case-study]**
> *Posh Pets Spain (PPS)* is a pet hotel in the village of Alhaurin el Grande, Spain. It is run by Rachel Goutorbe, an animal enthusiast, and her team of four pet specialists. *PPS* offers overnight accommodation with room for seven dogs or cats, a pet grooming service and a shop selling pet products, such as dog coats and dog leads. Pet grooming involves washing, cutting and combing a pet’s coat.

*PPS *is looking to improve its revenue and is considering two options:

- **Option 1: **trial a new brand of dog food in the shop
- **Option 2:** sponsor a local dog show.

Justify which **one **of these two options PPS should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
Revenue means the total amount of money a business earns from selling its products and services** [K]**

Trialling a new brand of dog food in the shop could directly increase PPS's revenue** [K]**. Dog owners regularly need to buy food for their pets** [Ap]**, so if the new brand proves popular, PPS could earn repeat sales on a regular basis, giving the business a reliable new source of income **[An]**

However, trialling new dog food carries a financial risk** [K]**. If the product does not sell well, PPS could be left with unsold stock it has already paid for** [Ap]**, which would waste money and put pressure on the business's cash flow** [An]**

Sponsoring a local dog show would raise awareness of PPS among dog owners in the area** [K]**, who are exactly the type of customers PPS needs** [Ap]**. This could encourage more people to book grooming appointments or overnight accommodation, helping PPS to increase revenue across all of its services **[An]**

However, sponsorship does not guarantee that dog owners will actually visit PPS or make a booking** [K]**. The cost of sponsoring a show could be difficult for a small business to afford** [Ap]**, and if no new customers follow, PPS will have spent money without any improvement in revenue **[An]**

Overall, I think PPS should choose Option 1 **[E]**. Sponsorship may raise awareness but cannot guarantee new customers or immediate revenue **[E]**

> **[case-study]**
> *TUI *is a holiday business that has over 100 years of experience. It offers customers a variety of holidays including staying in hotels, and river and ocean-going cruises. There are many extras that it offers to holiday makers including: car hire, extensions to the holiday and arranging day trips at all its holiday destinations.
> 
> The business is well known and flies its customers to over 180 destinations around the world, including Greece, Turkey and Spain. It has 1,600 travel agencies and 27 million customers. Holidays can be booked by visiting a travel agency or online.
> 
> *TUI *has holidays to meet the needs of all its customers: families, children, couples and those with disabilities.

The travel market that *TUI* operates in is very competitive, with many different businesses offering the same holidays at the same venues. When *TUI* introduces a new holiday or experience it has to consider the pricing strategy it will use. For its new holiday destination in Sri Lanka it is considering two options:

- **Option 1:** competition pricing
- **Option 2:** promotional pricing.

Justify which **one **of these two options *TUI *should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
A pricing strategy is the method a business uses to set the price of its products or services** [K]**

Competition pricing means setting prices at a similar level to rival companies ** [K]**. As many businesses offer the same holidays at the same venues **[Ap]**, matching competitor prices means customers who compare prices online are unlikely to choose a rival over TUI, helping TUI to remain competitive in a crowded market** [An]**

However, competition pricing gives customers no special reason to choose TUI's new Sri Lanka destination** [K]** **[Ap]**. If prices are the same as rivals, customers may simply book with a brand they already know, making it harder for TUI to attract bookings to a brand new destination **[An]**

Promotional pricing would allow TUI to launch Sri Lanka at a lower introductory price** [K]**, which could attract its 27 million existing customers who may not have considered visiting Sri Lanka before  **[Ap]**, quickly generating early bookings and raising awareness of the new destination **[An]**

However, promotional pricing reduces TUI's profit margin during the promotional period** [K]**. Once prices return to normal, some customers may be unwilling to pay the higher price, meaning TUI could struggle to maintain the same number of bookings **[Ap] **after the promotion ends **[An]**

Overall, TUI should choose Option 2 **[E]**. Sri Lanka is a completely new destination for TUI **[Ap]**, so promotional pricing is the best way to attract first-time bookings and generate interest in the new holiday **[An]**. Competition pricing gives customers no extra reason to choose TUI over a rival for a destination they have never seen TUI offer before **[E]**

*Saha *is planning to develop a new range of robots aimed at helping people in the home with cleaning, shopping, security and entertainment.

- **Option 2: **cost plus pricing.

Justify which **one **of these two options *Saha *should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
A pricing strategy is the method a business uses to set the price of its products **[K]**

Price skimming means setting a high launch price and reducing it over time **[K]**. Overall, Saha should choose Option 1 **[E]**. Home robots are innovative new technology** [Ap]**, and price skimming will generate strong early revenue to help fund Saha's plans to become a multinational within five years **[An]**. Cost plus pricing does not reflect the premium nature of the product and may not earn enough to support this growth **[E]**

> **[case-study]**
> The *LEGO *Group is a privately-owned business in Denmark. The business was founded in 1932 by the Kristiansen family. The family still owns it. The name *LEGO *is an abbreviation of two Danish words, ‘leg godt’ which means ‘play well’. It is now one of the world’s largest manufacturers of toys with 15 factories and over 18,000 employees around the world.
> 
> *LEGO *manufactures toys, games and art materials for boys and girls of all ages, and products from films such as Star Wars and Harry Potter. It believes that children are the role models of the future and playing with *LEGO* can support children in a developing and complex world.

*LEGO *is constantly introducing new toys to the market to keep its customers buying. It is planning to introduce a new Star Wars Princess Leia toy. It is considering the following two pricing strategies to launch the toy.

- **Option 1:** cost plus
- **Option 2:** skimming.

Justify which **one** of these two options *LEGO *should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
A pricing strategy is the method a business uses to decide how much to charge for its products **[K]**

Cost plus pricing ensures LEGO covers all of its production costs and makes a profit on every Princess Leia toy it sells **[K]**. As a large manufacturer with 15 factories **[Ap]**, LEGO can calculate its costs accurately and set a reliable selling price, giving the business financial security when launching a new product** [An]**

However, cost plus pricing may not take advantage of how popular the Star Wars brand is with customers **[K]**. If LEGO's production costs are low, the resulting selling price could be lower than what dedicated Star Wars fans are actually willing to pay **[Ap]**, meaning LEGO could miss out on higher revenue **[An]**

Price skimming would allow LEGO to launch the Princess Leia toy at a high price to target dedicated Star Wars fans and collectors **[K]**. These customers are often willing to pay a premium to be the first to own a new licensed toy **[An]**, helping LEGO to earn maximum revenue in the early stages of the launch **[Ap]**

However, a high launch price may put off families with children who buy LEGO toys as everyday gifts **[K] [Ap]**. Price-sensitive customers may wait until the price drops or choose a cheaper toy instead, which could limit the number of sales LEGO makes at launch **[An]**

LEGO should choose Option 2 **[E]**. The Star Wars Princess Leia toy is a licensed product from one of the world's most popular film franchises **[Ap]**, and dedicated fans and collectors are likely to pay a premium price to be first to own it **[An]**. Cost plus pricing would not reflect the popularity of the product and may mean LEGO earns less revenue than it could **[E]**

- **Option 2:** selling at the same price as competitors.

parts.solutionMd:

Offering a low introductory price for three months would encourage customers to try NOF pop for the first time **[K]**. Selling at the same price as competitors means NOF pop would be immediately competitive on the shelves of local retailers **[K]**. Customers who see NOF pop alongside other popcorn brands  **[Ap] **would not be put off by a higher price, making it easier for the product to compete from the day it launches **[An]**

However, as NOF pop is a new and unknown product **[K]** **[Ap]**, selling it at the same price as established brands gives customers no extra reason to try it [An]. Shoppers who already trust a rival brand may simply stick with what they know, making it harder for NOF to generate early sales **[An]**

Overall, NOF should choose Option 1 **[E]**. NOF pop is a brand new product and customers need a reason to try it for the first time **[Ap]**. A low introductory price creates that reason and could quickly build a loyal customer base **[An]**. Once customers enjoy the popcorn, many are likely to keep buying it even when the price rises after three months **[E]**

> - Emirates operates over 265 aircraft flying to more than 180 destinations → the high cost of maintaining this fleet means reducing ticket prices through special offers could seriously reduce profit → making social media advertising a more financially sustainable way to attract new passengers and rebuild market share

parts.problemMd: Define the term **diseconomies of scale**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award 1 mark for a correct definition of diseconomies of scale.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure you focus on the idea that average (unit) costs *increase* as the business grows. A common mistake is confusing diseconomies of scale with economies of scale — remember, diseconomies of scale are the opposite: they occur when a business becomes too large and efficiency falls, causing average costs to rise. **A** is incorrect because a purchasing economy of scale occurs when a business saves money by buying in bulk, which is not described here

**B** is incorrect because a financial economy of scale refers to a large business accessing cheaper borrowing, not communication problems

parts.problemMd: Explain **one** way in which technical economies of scale may reduce unit costs for a large business.
parts.solutionMd:
A large business can afford to invest in advanced or specialised machinery or technology **[1 mark]**. > Answers that list three ways technical economies of scale reduce unit costs with no explanation will get a maximum of 1 mark.

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Kova is a coffee chain founded in Tokyo, Japan in 2001. It began with a single café and has grown to operate over 3,000 cafés across 25 countries, serving over two million customers every day. Kova sources its coffee beans from farms in Colombia, Ethiopia and Vietnam, buying several thousand tonnes of coffee each year.
> 
> It employs over 60,000 staff worldwide and has a dedicated logistics team to manage the supply of ingredients to all its cafés. Kova's main competitors are well-established global coffee brands with similar scale and resources. Despite its size, Kova has managed to keep its prices lower than many rivals.

Evaluate the importance of economies of scale to Kova in keeping its prices competitive. You should use the information provided as well as your own knowledge of business.
parts.solutionMd:
Economies of scale occur when a business grows larger and its average cost per unit falls **[K]**

Economies of scale are very important to Kova because they allow it to buy coffee beans in very large quantities from farms in Colombia, Ethiopia and Vietnam **[Ap]**. As Kova purchases several thousand tonnes of coffee per year, suppliers are likely to offer significantly lower prices per tonne **[K]**, meaning Kova can keep its café prices lower than many rivals and attract more customers across its 25 countries of operation **[An]**

However, with over 3,000 cafés and 60,000 employees worldwide **[Ap]**, Kova may also experience diseconomies of scale **[K]**. Managing communication and maintaining consistent service standards across such a large global operation could become increasingly difficult, which may push up Kova's operating costs and reduce the benefit of its purchasing economies** [Ap] [An]**

Overall, economies of scale are very important to Kova** [E]**. Its ability to buy coffee at lower prices than smaller competitors is a key reason why it can keep its prices competitive while still making a profit **[An]**. Without this advantage, Kova would find it much harder to compete against well-established global coffee brands across 25 different countries **[Ap] [E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **12-mark 'evaluate' questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts linking points together to show clear cause and effect
>   - A clear, justified conclusion based on evaluation of the issues
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer  **
> 
> - Kova buys several thousand tonnes of coffee beans each year from farms in three different countries → suppliers are likely to offer significantly lower prices per tonne because of the size of Kova's orders → meaning Kova's cost per cup of coffee is lower than smaller rivals, allowing it to price competitively and attract more customers
> - Kova's dedicated logistics team manages the supply of ingredients to over 3,000 cafés worldwide → as Kova grows, it can spread the cost of this team across a larger number of cafés → reducing the logistics cost per café and helping Kova to keep its overall operating costs low
> - Managing over 60,000 staff and 3,000 cafés across 25 countries could lead to communication problems and inconsistent service standards → this diseconomy of scale could push up costs and damage Kova's reputation → which may offset some of the savings made through bulk purchasing of coffee beans

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Brio is a soft drinks manufacturer based in São Paulo, Brazil. It was founded in 1998 and now operates four factories, employing 12,000 workers. As Brio has grown, it has benefited from purchasing economies of scale, buying ingredients such as sugar and flavourings at significantly lower prices than smaller rivals.
> 
> However, in recent years Brio has also experienced diseconomies of scale. Communication between its head office and its four factories has become slower, and some factory managers have reported that workers feel poorly motivated and disconnected from the business.

Brio is considering two options:

- Option 1: open a fifth factory to increase production and achieve further economies of scale
- Option 2: close one factory to reduce the size of the business and improve efficiency.

Justify which one of these two options Brio should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
Economies of scale occur when a business grows and its average cost per unit of production falls **[K]**

Opening a fifth factory would allow Brio to increase production and achieve greater economies of scale **[K]**. By producing more soft drinks, Brio could negotiate even lower prices for ingredients like sugar and flavourings **[Ap]**, reducing its average production costs and helping it compete more effectively on price with rival soft drinks brands in South America **[An]**

However, opening a fifth factory would make Brio's operations even more complex to manage **[K]**. As Brio is already experiencing communication problems between its head office and four factories **[Ap]**, adding another factory could make these diseconomies of scale worse and further reduce worker motivation **[An]**

Closing one factory would make it easier for Brio to manage its remaining workforce and operations **[K]**. This could improve communication between the head office and factories, helping to re-motivate workers who currently feel disconnected from the business **[Ap]**, reducing inefficiencies and lowering average costs **[An]**

However, closing a factory would reduce Brio's production capacity and the purchasing economies of scale it currently benefits from **[K]**. With lower production volumes, Brio would buy smaller quantities of ingredients such as sugar **[Ap]**, meaning it could no longer negotiate the same low prices from suppliers, which would increase its average production costs **[An]**

Brio should choose Option 1 **[E]**. Its purchasing economies of scale are already a key competitive advantage **[Ap]**, and opening a fifth factory would strengthen this further **[An]**. The communication and motivation problems it currently faces can be addressed through better management practices without reducing the size of the business **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Opening a fifth factory would allow Brio to produce more soft drinks and buy larger quantities of ingredients like sugar and flavourings → suppliers would offer even lower prices per unit because of the larger order volume → reducing Brio's average production costs and strengthening its competitive position in the South American soft drinks market
> - Brio is already experiencing communication problems and falling worker motivation across its four factories → closing one factory would reduce the complexity of its operations → making it easier for managers to communicate clearly with workers and address the diseconomies of scale that are currently increasing costs
> - Reducing the size of the business by closing a factory would mean Brio buys smaller quantities of ingredients → this would reduce or eliminate the purchasing economies of scale it currently benefits from → meaning Brio's average costs could rise and it may struggle to compete on price with rival soft drinks brands in Brazil and South America

> - Chang Wei's ongoing leadership and decision-making continues to drive Pico's growth → his decisions to expand into 45 countries and win the international airline contract show the continuing importance of enterprise → meaning that even as the business has grown, the entrepreneur's vision remains central to its continued success

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Dusk is a furniture manufacturer based in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. It produces wooden tables, chairs and shelving units for export to retailers across Europe and Asia. The business employs 250 workers and currently uses a mix of traditional hand tools and some automated machinery in its production. Dusk has recently won a large new contract to supply furniture to a chain of hotels across Southeast Asia.

To fulfil this order, the business needs to significantly increase its output. It is considering two options:

- Option 1: invest in new automated machinery
- Option 2: hire an additional 80 workers.

Justify which one of these two options Dusk should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
Capital refers to the man-made resources such as machinery and equipment used in the production of goods** [K]**

Investing in new automated machinery would allow Dusk to increase its furniture production significantly and quickly **[K]**. As Dusk needs to fulfil a large contract supplying hotels across Southeast Asia **[Ap]**, automated machinery can produce tables, chairs and shelving units faster and more consistently than manual workers, helping Dusk to meet the order on time and protect its new client relationship **[An]**

However, purchasing new automated machinery requires a large upfront investment **[K]**. As Dusk currently uses a mix of hand tools and some machinery **[Ap]**, the cost of installing advanced automated equipment could put significant pressure on the business's finances in the short term **[An]**

Hiring an additional 80 workers would give Dusk the extra labour it needs to increase production using its existing methods **[K]**. Workers can be trained relatively quickly in the skills needed to make Dusk's furniture, and maintaining a handcrafted approach may help preserve the quality that retailers across Europe and Asia value **[Ap]** **[An]**

However, taking on 80 additional workers would significantly increase Dusk's ongoing wage costs **[K]**. If the hotel contract ends after completion **[Ap]**, Dusk would be left paying wages for workers it no longer needs, creating a long-term financial burden for the business **[An]**

Overall, Dusk should choose Option 1** [E]**. Automated machinery can produce furniture at a higher volume and lower cost per unit than manual workers **[An]**, which is more suitable for fulfilling a large hotel contract **[Ap]**. Although the upfront cost is high, Dusk would avoid the ongoing wage costs of 80 extra workers, making it the more financially sustainable choice in the long run** [E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - New automated machinery can work continuously without breaks, unlike human workers → allowing Dusk to produce more furniture each day to meet the demands of the large hotel contract → which would help Dusk deliver the order on time and protect its reputation with the new client
> - Hiring 80 additional workers gives Dusk greater flexibility in how furniture is made → workers can adapt to different designs and customise pieces in ways that automated machinery cannot → which could help Dusk maintain the handcrafted quality valued by retailers in Europe and Asia
> - If the hotel contract is completed and no further large orders follow → Dusk would face high ongoing wage costs for 80 extra workers it no longer needs → making machinery the safer long-term investment as it can be used for future orders without the same ongoing running costs

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Helix is a pharmaceutical company based in Basel, Switzerland. Founded in 1972, it manufactures medicines and vaccines sold to hospitals and healthcare providers in over 80 countries. Helix employs 15,000 scientists, researchers and factory workers. It has invested heavily in state-of-the-art laboratories, automated production lines and specialist medical equipment, which it regularly upgrades to maintain the highest standards of precision and safety. Helix spends over €500 million each year on research and development to create new medicines. Its competitors include large pharmaceutical companies based in the USA, Germany and Japan.

Evaluate the importance of capital as a factor of production to Helix. You should use the information provided as well as your own knowledge of business.
parts.solutionMd:
Capital refers to the man-made resources such as machinery and equipment used in the production of goods and services **[K]**

Capital is very important to Helix because its state-of-the-art laboratories and automated production lines **[K] **allow it to manufacture medicines and vaccines to the highest standards of precision and safety** [Ap]**. Without this specialist equipment, Helix could not produce medicines that meet the strict quality requirements of hospitals in 80 countries, risking its reputation and its ability to compete with large pharmaceutical rivals in the USA, Germany and Japan** [An]**

However, the labour provided by Helix's 15,000 scientists, researchers and factory workers is also essential **[K]**. Helix spends over €500 million each year on research and development** [Ap]**, which relies heavily on the expertise of its human workforce rather than machinery alone **[An]**, suggesting that labour may be just as important as capital in enabling Helix to develop new medicines** [E]**

Overall, capital is extremely important to Helix **[E]**. Without advanced laboratories and automated production lines, Helix could not produce medicines safely at the scale needed to supply 80 countries** [Ap]**. While labour is also crucial, it is the combination of highly skilled scientists and world-class capital equipment that allows Helix to stay ahead of its global competitors **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **12-mark 'evaluate' questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts linking points together to show clear cause and effect
>   - A clear, justified conclusion based on evaluation of the issues
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Helix's automated production lines allow it to manufacture large quantities of medicines and vaccines to a consistent standard → without this capital equipment, it could not supply hospitals in 80 countries at the required scale → meaning capital is essential for generating the revenue needed to fund Helix's €500 million annual research budget
> - Helix's scientists and researchers provide the knowledge needed to develop new medicines → automated machinery cannot replace human judgement in pharmaceutical research and development → suggesting that labour is just as important as capital to Helix's ability to create and produce innovative products
> - Helix regularly upgrades its specialist equipment to maintain the highest safety standards → this ongoing investment in capital helps Helix meet strict regulations in different countries → meaning without continual investment in capital, Helix could lose licences to sell medicines and face serious legal and financial consequences

parts.problemMd: Explain **one **reason why a business would use batch production.
parts.solutionMd:
A business would use batch production when it needs to make a variety of similar products with some differences between them **[1 mark]**, such as a clothing manufacturer producing the same design of shirt in different sizes or colours **[1 mark]**, as batch production allows the business to switch between variations without needing a separate production line for each one, making it a more flexible and cost-effective method than setting up individual production runs **[1 mark]**

> - A business would use batch production to respond flexibly to different levels of customer demand **[1 mark]**, as it can produce a larger or smaller batch depending on how many orders it has received **[1 mark]**, meaning the business avoids producing too much stock that cannot be sold or too little stock that fails to meet customer needs **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> *Irsi Chocolatier *is a chocolate shop in Brussels, the capital city of Belgium. There are many other chocolate shops nearby. Opened in 1989 by the Corne family, the business now has four directors and three employees. Florent Corne is the Managing Director with three other family members as directors.* Irsi Chocolatier* opens from Tuesday till Saturday. The shop sells a variety of handmade chocolates and jelly fruit sweets. It delivers locally and has a website for information purposes only.

*Irsi Chocolatier *is planning to produce chocolate lollipops in different shapes and flavours.

Currently, handmade chocolates are made using batch production, and cakes for special occasions use job production.

To make the new chocolate lollipops, *Irsi Chocolatier *is considering using:

- **Option 1: **batch production
- **Option 2:** job production.

Justify which **one **of these two options *Irsi Chocolatier* should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
Batch production means making a set quantity of one product before switching to make a different product** [K]**

Batch production would allow Irsi Chocolatier to make a set number of lollipops in each shape and flavour before moving on to the next** [K]**. As Irsi already uses batch production successfully for its handmade chocolates **[Ap]**, the team would be familiar with this approach, making it an efficient and cost-effective way to produce the new lollipop range** [An]**

However, if a particular batch of lollipops does not sell quickly, Irsi may be left with unsold stock that could go to waste** [K]**. As Irsi is a small shop with only seven people in total **[Ap]**, it may not have the storage space or resources to keep large batches of lollipops fresh **[An]**

Job production would allow Irsi to make each lollipop to a customer's individual requirements, such as a specific shape or personalised flavour** [K]**. As Irsi already uses job production for special occasion cakes **[Ap]**, this could extend its premium bespoke service to lollipops and allow it to charge higher prices **[An]**

However, job production is time-consuming for a product like lollipops** [K]**. With only three employees **[Ap]**, Irsi would not be able to produce enough lollipops to meet regular demand in the shop using job production alone [An], making it an impractical method for this new product **[An]**

Overall, Irsi Chocolatier should choose Option 1 **[E]**. Lollipops in different shapes and flavours are well-suited to batch production, which Irsi already uses for its handmade chocolates **[Ap]**. Producing batches of each flavour and shape is far more practical for a small team **[An]**, and will allow Irsi to stock its shop efficiently while keeping costs manageable **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Batch production allows Irsi to produce lollipops in different shapes and flavours in separate runs → this is the same method Irsi already uses successfully for its handmade chocolates → meaning the small team of three employees can produce the lollipops efficiently without needing to learn a new production method
> - Job production would allow customers to order personalised lollipops for special occasions → Irsi already offers this bespoke service for cakes → meaning a personalised lollipop service could attract customers wanting unique gifts and allow Irsi to charge a premium price
> - With only three employees and a small shop in Brussels → producing lollipops using job production would be too slow to generate enough stock to meet daily demand in the shop → making batch production the more practical and financially sustainable choice for a small family business

parts.problemMd:
> **[case-study]**
> Vela is a sports clothing manufacturer based in Medellín, Colombia. It produces training kits, sports shoes and gym wear for professional sports teams and individual customers across South America. It employs 800 workers across two large factories. In recent years, demand for Vela's products has grown significantly and the business is struggling to keep up with orders. Product quality has also become inconsistent, with some customers complaining about faulty stitching and sizing errors.

Vela is considering two options to improve its production:

- Option 1: invest in robotic technology to automate parts of the manufacturing process
- Option 2: introduce Kaizen to encourage workers to suggest continuous small improvements.

Justify which one of these two options Vela should choose.
parts.solutionMd:
Robotics involves using automated machines to carry out production tasks that were previously done by workers** [K]**

Investing in robotic technology would help Vela to improve the consistency and quality of its sports clothing **[K]**. As customers have complained about faulty stitching and sizing errors **[Ap]**, robots can perform manufacturing tasks with greater precision than human workers, reducing the number of faulty products and helping Vela to rebuild customer confidence in its brand** [An]**

However, investing in robotic technology requires a large amount of money to set up **[K]**. For a business operating two factories and employing 800 workers **[Ap]**, the initial cost of purchasing and installing automated machinery could be very high, putting pressure on Vela's finances in the short term **[An]**

Introducing Kaizen would encourage all 800 of Vela's workers to suggest small improvements to the way clothing is made **[K]**. This could gradually improve quality as workers identify and fix problems such as stitching errors on the production line **[Ap]**, at a much lower cost than investing in new robotic technology **[An]**

However, Kaizen takes time to show results as improvements are made gradually and in small steps **[K]**. As Vela is already struggling to keep up with growing demand **[Ap]**, a slow improvement process may not solve its quality and production speed problems quickly enough **[An]**

Overall, Vela should choose Option 1 **[E]**. Customer complaints about faulty stitching and sizing errors suggest that a more immediate solution is needed **[Ap]**. Robotic technology can improve both quality and production speed at the same time **[An]**, whereas Kaizen relies on gradual change and may not be fast enough to meet Vela's urgent need to increase output and reduce faults** [E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Vela's customers have complained about faulty stitching and sizing errors → robotic technology can perform manufacturing tasks with much greater precision than human workers → directly addressing the quality problems and reducing the number of faulty products that reach customers
> - Introducing Kaizen would give all 800 of Vela's workers a voice in improving production → workers who feel their ideas are valued are likely to be more motivated and productive → which could gradually improve both quality and output without the high upfront cost of investing in robotic machinery
> - Vela is struggling to keep up with growing demand for its products → Kaizen relies on gradual incremental improvements that take time to have a significant effect → meaning Vela would continue to fall behind on orders while waiting for Kaizen to deliver results, making robotics the more effective immediate solution

As a global food brand selling in many different countries **[Ap]**, a serious quality or food safety failure could lead to a product recall affecting hundreds of millions of packets **[An]**, which would cost far more than the expense of its quality control team and could permanently damage customer trust in the brand** [E]**
